chunk_findings.detail: `depth` computes the number of ancestors between an item and its phase/root, then unconditionally truncates the result to 6. Depth is a property of well-formed input, not only of the malformed cycles the comment cites: for a phase `P` with a legitimate chain `P → t1 → t2 → t3 → t4 → t5 → t6 → t7` (each task's `parent` being the previous one), `closure`/`above` yields 7 ancestors, but `depth` returns `min(7, 6) == 6`. `board_rows` feeds that value straight into the markdown indentation and into the `"depth"` field of `board --json` (via `rows(...)`), so a task nested more than six levels below its phase is rendered at the wrong indent level (and reports the wrong depth in JSON). The whole point of this change is that the board must stay byte-identical while the tallies are recomputed in core; this new, silent cap changes the board for any hierarchy deeper than six, and the `min(..., 6)` is not what protects against cycles anyway — a parent cycle is handled by `closure`'s own visited-set (the `last.parent == last.id` term only reacts to a cycle that has already terminated), so the bound only ever bites legitimate deep nesting.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/progress.py:depth (`return min(len(above) + (last.parent == last.id != root), 6)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
`progress.tally` is documented by the inline comment as counting at *every depth* ("the one phase rule: every depth, abandoned out"), i.e. it descends into sub-tasks of the tasks it is handed. The old code counted exactly the elements of `q.tasks_under(p.id)` (minus abandoned) and compared `n_done == len(tasks)`, and the `tasks`/`rows` list used for rendering is still taken directly from `under`. So when a phase has a nested sub-task, `n.live` and `n.done` no longer equal `len(tasks)` / `n_done`.

Concrete failure: a phase marked `DONE` whose direct tasks are all `DONE` but which has one nested sub-task still `RUNNING`. Old: `n_done == len(tasks)` is true, so the phase hits the `done += 1; continue` short-circuit and produces only a phase count. New: `n.done != n.live`, so the branch is skipped and a phase card is emitted, with `done`/`total` that include the nested task that never appears in `tasks`/`rows`. This changes `board --json`/markdown output for any hierarchy with nested sub-tasks, contradicting the stated invariant that those outputs must be byte-identical (this change is not in the list of the three permitted visible changes). The same divergence applies to `"done": n.done, "total": n.live` on non-done phases, where the card total can now exceed the number of rendered rows.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor drops the explicit non-empty guard that the old expression carried. Previously the test was `c := _phase_counts(items, p.id))[1] and c[0] == c[1]`, i.e. a phase was only "ready to close" if it had at least one live task child (`total != 0`) *and* all of them were done. The replacement is just `... and PR.phase_tally(st, p.id).complete`, and per the comment on the line above, `phase_tally` deliberately excludes abandoned tasks from the total. For a phase that is not DONE but has zero non-abandoned tasks — a freshly created phase, or a phase whose tasks were all marked ABANDONED — `phase_tally` yields `done == 0`, `live == 0`, so a `complete` predicate of the natural shape `done == live` evaluates to True. The progress line then appends `, N ready to close` for a phase that has nothing left to close, whereas the old code suppressed it (the `c[1]` term was falsy). This is a fourth visible change, not one of the three intended ones (B01281f654e/Bb24939611d/B45b55be6a4), so the progress line is no longer byte-identical to before for any state containing an empty or fully-abandoned phase. The every-depth counting intended by Bb24939611d is achieved by `phase_tally`'s recursion; the non-empty guard it replaced needs to be preserved (or `Tally.complete` must be defined as `live > 0 and done == live`) to avoid the spurious "ready to close".

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own rule block states that a phase's tasks are its *live* tasks and that "an abandoned task is SETTLED, not outstanding", so a phase cannot close only "while any of them is open". With `complete = self.live > 0 and self.done == self.live`, a phase whose every task is abandoned yields `Tally(done=0, live=0, abandoned=N)` and therefore `complete is False` — even though no live task is open, exactly the situation the rule says is settled. Concretely, `tally([t_state == ABANDONED])` returns `Tally(0, 0, 1)` and `Tally(0, 0, 1).complete` is `False`, so any consumer using `complete` to render a phase as done/ready-to-close (phase list / progress line) will keep such a phase open forever. The `live > 0` guard conflates "no live work left" with "never had any work"; dropping the guard (testing `done == live` directly) would make an all-abandoned phase settle as the rule describes.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old expression pinned the emitted order to `_ORDER = (DONE, RUNNING, REVIEW, OPEN, BLOCKED, ABANDONED)`:
`[{"state": s, "n": counts[s]} for s in _ORDER if counts[s]]`. The new one iterates `counts.items()`, i.e. whatever order `progress.state_counts()` happens to produce. Nothing in the diff guarantees that order. A natural implementation (`{}` built in first-encountered order, or `collections.Counter`) emits states in task-encounter order, not the canonical `_ORDER`. Concrete case: a project whose only two tasks appear in the store as RUNNING then DONE yields `task_counts == [{"state": RUNNING, ...}, {"state": DONE, ...}]`, whereas before it was `[{"state": DONE, ...}, {"state": RUNNING, ...}]`. `status --json` is then no longer byte-identical to the golden, and this is not one of the three allowed visible changes (phase list, progress sub-task depth, progress phase name).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/kind_status.py:_data (`task_counts`)

chunk_findings.detail: `counts[DONE]` used to be unconditionally safe: `counts = {s: sum(...) for s in _ORDER}` always created a `DONE` key. The replacement `progress.state_counts(tasks)` has no such contract stated anywhere; if it returns only the states that actually occur (the obvious `Counter(t.state for t in tasks)` shape), then any project with zero completed tasks makes `counts[DONE]` raise `KeyError`, crashing the `status` export. Input that demonstrates it: `tasks` containing only RUNNING/OPEN tasks (or an empty project) -> `state_counts` has no `DONE` entry -> `KeyError: DONE` on this line. Note the retained `if n` filter on `task_counts` is exactly the "drop zero counts" behaviour that suggests zero entries are otherwise present, but the subscript on the very next statements assumes they are present for `DONE` — the two assumptions conflict unless `state_counts` materialises every state.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor replaces `epoch(r["at"])` (from `core.progress`) with `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`, i.e. it newly asserts that naive timestamps be interpreted in the host's local zone. This is a semantic change, not a formatting one, so it is outside what `tests/test_clock_format.py` pins ("minute/date slices, age renderings, the now writers"). The run records it parses are written by `schedule.py`, which now stamps them with `clock.now_utc()` — a UTC instant — so their naive wall-clock text is UTC, and reading it back as *local* shifts every timestamp by the host's UTC offset. Concrete case: a run at 12:00 UTC stored as `...T12:00:00`, read on a UTC−05:00 host, becomes epoch for 17:00Z, i.e. `last` is 5 h too large; then `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is 5 h too small, so a cadence sitting on its period boundary is reported as *not* due, and for the due ones `since` renders a smaller `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)` value (e.g. "6.8 days" instead of "7.0 days"). Both the due/not-due decision and the rendered `since` string therefore differ from the pre-refactor output on any non-UTC host — the byte-identical guarantee fails, and no test in the formatting suite covers it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/operations.py (`clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`)

chunk_findings.detail: The original expression floored whole minutes: `f"{w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`. The new call passes only the seconds and relies on `clock.fmt_age`'s default formatting. Compare the sibling migrations in this same diff: every place that reproduced a `secs / 60:.1f` rendering explicitly passes `places=1` (`cli.py` `held` and the attempt line). The lifecycle site is the only one that dropped its argument, and its old expression was a `// 60` floor, not a decimal/rounding format. If the helper's default does what the `places` parameter name implies — format `f"{s / 60:.{places}f}m"` with a default decimal count — the string is no longer byte-identical for any waiting time that is not an exact multiple of 60: with `waiting_s = 100` the old code emits `1m` (`100 // 60 == 1`) while `f"{100/60:.0f}m"` emits `2m`; with `waiting_s = 90` the old code emits `1m` while `f"{90/60:.0f}m"` emits `2m`. Changing `// 60` to a division-and-format helper silently replaces floor with rounding, so the "every output must stay byte-identical" contract is broken on this line unless `fmt_age` special-cases a floored default, which the caller does not request.

chunk_findings.detail: The refactor does not just rename the helper: `epoch(r["at"])` (no keyword) became `clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local")`, which hard-codes how offset-less timestamps are decoded. The run timestamps in `runs` are written by the same clock helpers that write UTC (cf. `at = given or clock.now_utc()` in `schedule.py`, and the `%H:%M:%SZ` UTC rendering), so any log entry serialized without a `+00:00` offset — which the intent says must keep producing byte-identical output — is now interpreted in the process's local timezone rather than whatever the old `progress.epoch` default did. Concretely, with `TZ=America/New_York` and a run stored as `"2024-01-01T10:00:00"` (10:00 UTC), the decoded `last` moves by +5h (05:00 UTC), so `age_days = (now - last)/86400` is off by ~0.21 days; for a daily cadence near the `age_days >= days` boundary this flips the `due` verdict and also changes the `"since"` string emitted via `clock.fmt_age(now - last, "days", places=1)`. The format-pinning test `tests/test_clock_format.py` only pins rendering, not this decoding, so it would not catch the shift. The change is output-preserving only if the removed `progress.epoch` already defaulted to local; if its default was UTC (consistent with the rest of the module writing UTC), this is a regression.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/operations.py:_due (the `last = max((clock.epoch(r["at"], naive="local") ...` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The old code inserted `lease.ttl_s // 60` directly into the f-string (`past its {lease.ttl_s // 60} min TTL`). For an `int` TTL this is an `int`, and the new code matches. But `clock.fmt_age` wraps the quotient in `int(...)`, whereas the old TTL expression had no `int()`. So for a non-integer `ttl_s` (e.g. a TTL read from config/JSON as a float), the rendered text changes: with `lease.ttl_s = 90.0`, the old line rendered `past its 1.0 min TTL` (`90.0 // 60 == 1.0`, formatted by the f-string), while the new one renders `past its 1 min TTL` (`int(90.0 // 60) == 1`). The same applies to any float TTL (e.g. `ttl_s = 600.0` → `10.0 min` becomes `10 min`). The `idle` and `ago` values are unaffected because their original expressions already applied `int(...)` (`int((now - lease.renewed_at) // 60)` and `max(0, int(... // 60))`), so only this third, newly-`int()`-wrapped TTL value is a behavior change. If TTLs can ever be non-integral seconds, the promised byte-identity does not hold.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/enforce.py:1029 (`ttl = clock.fmt_age(lease.ttl_s, "min")`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old `_now()` was a function defined in `rules.py` whose body called `datetime.now(UTC)` at *call* time. The replacement `_now = clock.now_utc` is a module-level **alias** that captures whatever function object `clock.now_utc` was at import time, so it no longer follows the `clock` module. Concretely: in an environment where time is frozen by replacing the clock (e.g. `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.clock, "now_utc", lambda: FIXED)` — or any production wiring that swaps the clock), `gates/runner.py`'s `compact_at` is re-imported and re-resolved per call and will stamp the frozen time into log filenames, while `rules._now()` keeps returning the real wall clock and writes real timestamps into the rule data, so two "now" writers in the same process disagree. This is also inconsistent with the way the other three sites invoke their helper (`clock.fmt_minute(...)`, `clock.iso_at(...)`, `compact_at()`) rather than pre-binding it. The fix is to keep a thin call-through (`def _now(): return clock.now_utc()`) or to call `clock.now_utc()` directly wherever `_now` is used.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/rules.py (`_now = clock.now_utc`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old expression was `f"... {w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`, i.e. floor division that always yields whole minutes. It has been replaced with `clock.fmt_age(w['waiting_s'])`, dropping the explicit floor. For the two call sites that pass an explicit `places=1` the replacement is the same arithmetic (`secs / 60` formatted to 1 decimal), which shows `fmt_age` takes raw seconds and renders `seconds / 60` with `places` decimals. With the default `places=0` that is `f"{secs/60:.0f}m"`, which *rounds* rather than truncates. Given `waiting_s = 90` the old line printed `... 1m so far`, the new one prints `... 2m so far` (1.5 rounds to 2); given `waiting_s = 3599` the old line printed `59m`, the new one prints `60m` (59.983 → 60). Any caller/test that only exercises multiples of 60 (or only the `places=1` path) will not notice, but real `waiting_s` values are arbitrary, so the status output is not byte-identical to the old expression. To preserve the old string the call must floor before formatting (e.g. `fmt_age(w['waiting_s'] // 60 * 60)` or a floor/truncation mode), not rely on the default `places=0` rendering.

chunk_findings.detail: The old `_fmt_since` was a local `def`; the replacement is a module-level alias that binds the *function object* `clock.fmt_time` at import time rather than looking it up at call time. This is the exact defect that was confirmed and fixed for `rules._now = clock.now_utc` (finding 3): the project's tests/production wiring freeze or redirect time by swapping attributes on `ddflow.core.clock`, and a module-level alias silently keeps the original object. Concretely, `monkeypatch.setattr(ddflow.core.clock, "fmt_time", lambda t: "00:00:00Z")` (the same pattern the suite uses for `clock.now_utc`) followed by `reservations._reserved_msg(...)` still calls the pre-patch `fmt_time` and renders the real time-of-day, while every other refactored site in this diff (`brief.py`, `operations.py`, `schedule.py`) calls `clock.<helper>(...)` at call time and does follow the patch. It should be a `def _fmt_since(t): return clock.fmt_time(t)` (or an inline `clock.fmt_time` at the call sites), not an import-time alias.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/reservations.py:_fmt_since (`_fmt_since = clock.fmt_time`)

chunk_findings.detail: The previous review's item 4 is not answered by its probe, so I am re-raising it. The old expression was `f"... {w['waiting_s'] // 60}m so far"`, i.e. *floor division on the raw value*, and `//` on a float yields a float that the f-string renders with a decimal. Given `w['waiting_s'] = 119.9`, the old code renders `1.0m`; the new code renders `int(119.9 // 60)` → `1m`. Likewise `waiting_s = 3599.9` rendered `59.0m` before and `59m` now. The triage's probe does not refute this: it asserts `fmt_age(s) == f'{int(s) // 60}m'` for `s = 119.9, 3599`, but `f'{int(s) // 60}m'` is a restatement of the *new* function's behavior, not of the *old* expression (`f'{s // 60}m'`), which for those same inputs is `1.0m`/`59.0m`. So the test named "matches_every_old_rendering" compares the helper to itself and never demonstrates equivalence for non-integer input. Unlike the `ttl_s` refutation (which cited `ttl_s=int(...)` in `core/handlers/leases.py`), no evidence is given that `waiting_s` is always an `int`; if the API computes it via `total_seconds()` (or any non-int path) without truncation, the two renderings diverge exactly as shown, so the floor-vs-float difference is a real output regression that the probe does not address.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is advertised as keeping "the expressions core.clock replaced" from growing back (`"""...A guard keeps the expressions from growing back elsewhere."""`, and the test is named `test_the_replaced_expressions_live_only_in_core_clock`), but `_BANNED` only covers two of the three replaced expressions: it bans the `fmt_minute` form (`\[:16\]\.replace\(...T...`) and `datetime.now(...)`, and never bans `fmt_date`'s replaced expression `ts[:10]`. Demonstration: appending `_x = "2026-10-07T01:02:03Z"[:10]` to e.g. `ddflow/services/rules.py` leaves `test_the_replaced_expressions_live_only_in_core_clock` green, even though the exact slice `fmt_date` was introduced to replace is now duplicated outside `core/clock.py` — i.e. the invariant the test (and module docstring) claims to enforce is false. (The same escape applies to a plain `[:16]` minute truncation written without `.replace("T"`, since the regex requires the `.replace("T"` suffix.) This is a test-only gap with no runtime impact, hence LOW.

chunk_findings.detail: In the success branch, `_decode(out, "replace" if raw else errors).strip()` and the same for `stderr` decode git's raw output with `errors="strict"` whenever the caller did not pass `z=True`/`binary=True` and did not override `errors`. Git emits many outputs as raw, non-transcoded bytes: commit messages and author/committer fields (`git log --format=%s`), blob contents (`git show <rev>:<path>`), and diff bodies are all printed verbatim, and even path names are printed verbatim when `core.quotePath=false`. A single byte that is not valid UTF-8 therefore raises `UnicodeDecodeError` *out of* `run` — it is not an `OSError` or `P.TimeoutExpired`, so neither `except` clause catches it, and the caller gets an exception instead of the `GitResult` the module promises. Concrete input: a repository whose HEAD commit subject was created with `git commit -m "$(printf 'caf\xe9')"` (Latin-1), then `run(repo, "log", "-1", "--format=%s")` — `p.stdout` is `b"caf\xe9\n"`, and `_decode(out, "strict")` raises on byte `0xe9`. This is precisely the failure mode `git_paths` was introduced to eliminate (the docstring's own history: "ONE non-UTF-8 name anywhere raised out of the caller -- every commit ... failed"), and the module docstring's contract that a git call is never an exception for "could not tell" is violated for the default text path; the fix is to default `errors` to `"replace"` (or always use a forgiving codec) for the non-raw case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/git.py: `run()` default `errors="strict"`

chunk_findings.detail: The local `GitResult` that this alias replaces carried a field that is specific to this merge module: `attempted: bool = True`, documented as "False when a precondition refused the merge before git tried to merge the branch (the target is missing, checked out elsewhere, or another merge is in progress): the item's own branch was not judged, so it is not a failed merge of that branch." A *shared* runner result (`infra.git`'s `GitResult`, also used by `services/ci.py`, `services/flow.py`, `services/version_files.py`, none of which have any merge concept) does not model that distinction, yet the alias makes `GitResult` here be exactly that foreign class. Nothing in this diff adjusts the merge path that uses it, so the unchanged call sites in this same file still do `return GitResult(code, out, err, attempted=False)` on a precondition refusal and still branch on `res.attempted`. Concretely, when a merge precondition refuses (e.g. the target branch is checked out in another worktree), that constructor now raises `TypeError: __init__() got an unexpected keyword argument 'attempted'`, and any caller reading `res.attempted` raises `AttributeError` — the "not attempted, do not mark the item as a failed merge" path crashes (or, if the field were silently dropped rather than rejected, misclassifies the item as a failed merge of its own branch), which is precisely the behavior the removed field existed to encode.

chunk_findings.detail: The old body explicitly bounded this git invocation with `timeout=300` and translated `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` into `None` ("could not tell"). The rewrite forwards no `timeout` at all, so the call now runs under whatever default `git.run` uses. That default cannot be assumed to be 300s: it is the general replacement for the `P.run(["git", ...])` calls in this same changeset (`flow.py`, `version_files.py`), which all relied on the (short) `P.run` default, while `_git_z` deliberately overrode it — precisely because tree fingerprinting runs `git ls-files`/`git status` over a whole worktree and needs more headroom than the quick `diff`/`show`/`patch-id` calls. Concretely, on a large repository (or a repo on a slow/stalled mount) where the paths-listing command exceeds the default, `_git_z` now returns `None` (or, if the new default is "no timeout", blocks ddflow indefinitely) where the pre-change code returned the decoded path list after up to 300s. The downstream tree fingerprint / gate evidence therefore degrades from a real fingerprint to "could not tell". The call should preserve the bound, e.g. `GIT.run(cwd, *args, timeout=300, binary=True).paths()`.

chunk_findings.detail: Only `P.TimeoutExpired` and `OSError` are caught around the child-bytes path, but `_decode` is invoked with the caller's `errors` value, which defaults to `"strict"`. Any non-UTF-8 byte in the child's stdout (or stderr) therefore raises `UnicodeDecodeError` — a `ValueError`, not an `OSError` — straight out of `run()`, defeating the module's promise that git trouble is reported as a `GitResult` (`unavailable=True`), and giving text-mode callers in `services/ci.py`, `services/flow.py`, `services/version_files.py` no way to distinguish "could not tell" from a crash. Concrete input: in a repo whose `HEAD:data.txt` contains `b"caf\xe9\n"`, `git.run(repo, "show", "HEAD:data.txt")` returns raw stdout containing `0xe9`; `_decode(out, "strict")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError` instead of returning `GitResult(0, ...)`. The same happens via `err` for a failing call whose message embeds a non-UTF-8 path, and for `git log`/`git diff` text output (which, unlike pathnames under `core.quotepath`, git does not C-quote — so `-z` is no protection here; only `z`/`binary` callers get `"replace"`). The fix would be to decode text output with `"replace"`/`"surrogateescape"` (or wrap the decode in the same except and set `unavailable`), so that undecodable output is a `GitResult` rather than an escaping exception.

chunk_findings.detail: The old body returned `None` whenever git failed (`returncode != 0`, `OSError` or `TimeoutExpired`), and the docstring — still present in the changed hunk — documents that contract ("or None when git failed -- 'could not tell', never 'nothing'"). The new body is `return GIT.run(cwd, *args, binary=True).paths()`, which never inspects `.ok`/`returncode` before calling `.paths()`. `.paths()` is a decoder over `out_bytes`; when the call is unavailable/timed out/non-zero, `out_bytes` is empty, so `.paths()` yields `[]` rather than `None`. That silently converts "git could not tell" into "there are no files". Concretely, calling `_git_z` on a `cwd` that is not inside a git work tree (or where `git ls-files ...` exits non-zero) used to return `None`; it now returns `[]`, so `tree_fingerprint` (and anything else that branches on `is None`) computes a fingerprint over an empty/partial file set and reports a wrong `tree` digest to the gate evidence instead of falling back. The `binary=True` argument only avoids the strict-decode problem; it does nothing to preserve the `ok`-check that the removed code performed.

chunk_findings.detail: The call site asks `GIT.run(..., binary=True)` precisely so it gets the raw blob bytes in `out_bytes`, then decodes them with the strict default `.decode("utf-8")` and no `try/except`. This re-introduces the exact failure mode the previous review flagged for `git.py:run`: a `UnicodeDecodeError` (a `ValueError`, neither `OSError` nor a `VersionFileError`) escapes the service instead of git trouble being reported as a `GitResult` / handled failure. Concrete input: a version file containing a non-UTF-8 byte, e.g. a byte `0xFF` anywhere in the blob, makes `git show {ref}:{path}` succeed with `ok=True`, then `(shown.out_bytes or b"")` is `b'...\xff...'` and `.decode("utf-8")` raises `UnicodeDecodeError`, which propagates out of this function rather than being converted to `VersionFileError` like the `not shown.ok` branch above. The previous finding's fix lives inside `run()` (it only selects `errors="replace"` when it decodes `out`/`err` itself for raw/binary capture); because this caller bypasses that by using `out_bytes` and decoding on its own, the fix does not answer this path. The decode needs `errors=` handling or a wrap into `VersionFileError`.

chunk_findings.detail: `run_shell` builds the subprocess kwargs with `text=True, errors="replace"` but never pins `encoding`, so on the normal (completed) path `subprocess` decodes the child's stdout/stderr with the locale encoding (`locale.getpreferredencoding(False)`). On the timeout path, the captured bytes come straight out of `subprocess.TimeoutExpired.output/.stderr` (CPython joins the raw pipe chunks with `b''.join(...)`, so those fields are `bytes` even in text mode), and `_text` decodes them with a hardcoded `"utf-8"`. The same bytes are therefore decoded with two different codecs depending on whether the command timed out. Concrete input/environment: on a host whose preferred encoding is not UTF-8 (Windows default cp1252, or `LANG=C`/`LC_ALL=C` on Linux), a command that prints a non-ASCII byte and then exceeds `timeout_s` — e.g. cp1252 `0xE9` for `é` — yields `"\ufffd"` (or two `"\ufffd"` under C locale) in `ShellResult.out` on timeout, while the identical command completed normally yields `"é"`. Callers that parse or compare output get different results purely because the command was killed at its bound. The fix is to pin `encoding="utf-8"` for the subprocess call (so both paths agree) or to decode the timeout bytes with the same encoding the wrapper used for the completed case.

chunk_findings.detail: The old check read the child's stderr (`_looks_like_not_found(p.stderr or "")`), and the code comment above it still says the shell reports "command not found" *on stderr*. The new code inspects `p.err` instead, but `p.err` is also the field used one branch earlier as the text for `"could not execute: {p.err}"` — i.e. it is the execution/spawn-error field, set when the process never started. Those two uses are mutually exclusive: a process that starts and exits 127 never fails to spawn, so `p.err` is empty (or `None`) in exactly the case this branch is trying to detect, while the shell's "sh: line 1: foo: command not found" text is part of the merged `p.output` that was just assigned to `out`. The concrete failure is a compound gate command such as `gdef.command = "nope | tee log"` (pre-flight cannot inspect pipes): the shell runs, writes the not-found diagnostic to stderr, exits 127, `p.code in (126, 127)` is true, but `_looks_like_not_found(p.err)` is false because `p.err` holds nothing, so the gate is reported as an ordinary failed command with `"exit": 127` instead of `"unavailable"`, changing the retry/abort decision. In the variant where `err` is `None`, `p.err.strip()[:200]` in the same branch raises `AttributeError` and takes down the gate runner, whereas `subprocess` gave `""` and the old code guarded with `(p.stderr or "")`. Either the diagnostic must come from `p.output` (the merged child output) or `p.err` must not be reused as the spawn-error text.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py (`if p.code in (126, 127) and _looks_like_not_found(p.err)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The `try` in `run_shell` wraps the entire `_shell_group(...)` call, and `_shell_group` invokes the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback repeatedly on this thread while the command runs. Any `ValueError` or `OSError` raised *by that callback* is therefore caught and converted into `ShellResult(None, err=str(exc), could_not_run=True)` — i.e. the result claims the command never started, even though it did start and may still be running. This is a plausible real path: `on_tick` is used to renew a lease during long gates, and a lease renewal that fails with a network error raises an `OSError`/`ConnectionError` (a subclass of `OSError`). Given that input, `run_shell` returns `could_not_run=True` and the caller silently treats a live command / transient network failure as "the command could not be run" (the exact meaning the `ShellResult` docstring attaches to a missing tool or refused environment), instead of surfacing the callback's bug. It also contradicts `run_shell`'s own docstring, which insists that caller bugs around `on_tick` "still raise ValueError". The exception scope should be narrowed to the command's own launch failure (e.g. catch only around `Popen`/spawn), or `on_tick` failures should be allowed to propagate.

chunk_findings.detail: The old code built the recorded output from both streams: `out = (p.stdout or "") + (p.stderr or "")`. The new code sets `out = p.output`, and the result object exposes stderr separately as `p.err` (that is exactly the field used just below for not-found detection and for the `could_not_run` message). With `output` meaning the process' stdout, any gate whose diagnostics are written to stderr silently disappears from the recorded result: the subsequent `"output_digest": digest(out)` and `"output_bytes": len(out)` now reflect stdout only. Concrete case: a gate command `sh -c 'echo "warning: X" 1>&2; exit 0'` produced `out == "warning: X\n"` before (digest non-empty, `output_bytes > 0`) and now produces `out == ""` (`digest("")`, `output_bytes == 0`). Any consumer that compares `output_digest` to detect whether a gate's output changed, or that reports `output_bytes`, will treat runs that differ only on stderr as identical. If the intent of the new API was stdout+stderr, this should be `out = p.output + (p.err or "")`; if the intent was stdout-only, the digest/bytes consumers downstream need to be made aware, because their input just changed for every stderr-emitting gate.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old body sent the signal with the child's pid *used directly as the process-group id*:
`os.killpg(thing.pid, signal.SIGKILL)`. The replaced code in `onboard_verify._stop`, by contrast, resolved the group with `os.killpg(os.getpgid(proc.pid), ...)`. Those two are not equivalent once the group leader is gone: if the shell (the session/group leader, started with `start_new_session=True`) has already exited while the reviewer it spawned is still alive, `os.getpgid(thing.pid)` raises `ProcessLookupError`, whereas `os.killpg(thing.pid, ...)` still succeeds because the group id remains valid as long as any member lives. If the shared `P.kill_group` is implemented the way the two other refactored call sites were (resolve via `os.getpgid`, fall back to `proc.kill()`), then in the scenario "reviewer shell exited (or daemonized its child), reviewer still running, `_abort(thing)` called", the `getpgid` lookup fails, the `proc.kill()` fallback is a no-op (the Popen is already reaped / the pid is gone), and the reviewer `_abort` was specifically written to kill — "the shell AND the reviewer it started" — survives. The old `os.killpg(thing.pid, ...)` form would have delivered SIGKILL to that surviving group member. The call site was changed to the shared helper without preserving the pid-as-pgid semantics it relied on.

The old code built the gate's captured output as `out = (p.stdout or "") + (p.stderr or "")`; the new code replaces it with `out = p.output`. Concrete input: a gate command such as `sh -c 'echo A; echo B >&2; exit 1'` previously yielded `out == "A
B
"`, now yields `out == "A
"`. As a result `ev["output_digest"] = digest(out)` and `ev["output_bytes"] = len(out)` no longer change when only the child's stderr changes, so a stderr-only change (e.g. a new diagnostic/failure message printed by a tool that keeps stdout identical) is recorded as an unchanged gate result and can be matched against — and satisfied by — a previously recorded outcome. chunk_findings.detail: The test claims (via its trailing `pytest.fail("the command outlived the failed tick")`) to prove the whole command was torn down when the tick callback raised, but the only thing it verifies is `os.kill(pid, 0)` where `pid` is `$$` — the PID of the `sh` that run_shell spawned. The command `echo $$ > {pidfile}; sleep 30` makes the shell fork a separate `sleep 30` child (dash/bash only `exec` the last command when it is the sole command), so if the tick-failure cleanup kills just the direct child (e.g. `proc.kill()` / `os.kill(shell_pid, SIGKILL)`) instead of the process group, the shell is killed and reaped, `os.kill(pid, 0)` raises `ProcessLookupError`, and the test returns green while `sleep 30` is left orphaned and running for its full 30 seconds. Because the change's stated purpose is to consolidate the "private killpg copies", no test in this file actually distinguishes `killpg` from `kill`, so a regression that drops process-group cleanup on the tick-error/exception path passes undetected; the test should capture and probe `$!`/the whole group (or assert on the group id), not just the shell's own PID.

chunk_findings.detail: The fix for the earlier tick-callback finding only guards the `except (OSError, ValueError)` branch with `if from_tick: raise`; the preceding `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch does not consult `from_tick` at all. `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` is a `SubprocessError`, i.e. not an `OSError`/`ValueError`, so if the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback raises it (a very natural thing for a lease-renewal callback that shells out to a CLI or otherwise uses `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)`), `tick()` records it in `from_tick` and re-raises, it propagates out of `_shell_group`, and `run_shell` catches it here and returns `ShellResult(None, _text(exc.output), _text(exc.stderr), timed_out=True, ...)`. The caller is then told the *operator's command* timed out and was killed, when in fact the command may still be running normally and only the callback's own subprocess timed out — the same "attribute the callback's trouble to the command" defect that finding #1 was about, just through the other handler. The `if from_tick: raise` guard needs to be present in the `TimeoutExpired` branch as well (before returning the timed-out result).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:run_shell (`except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The old body wrapped the run in `try: ... except subprocess.TimeoutExpired ... except (OSError, ValueError) as exc: return "unavailable", {"reason": f"could not execute: {exc}", ...}`. The new body has no `except` at all: it assumes `run_shell` never raises and instead reports every failure through `p.timed_out` / `p.could_not_run`. But `run_shell` is invoked with `on_tick=on_tick` and runs that callback *on this thread* (that is the whole point of the ticking path). Prior finding #1 was confirmed precisely because a `ValueError`/`OSError` raised by `on_tick` was being swallowed into `could_not_run=False`; the fix for it stops `run_shell` from mislabeling such an error, which means the error is no longer contained inside `run_shell` either. With the gate-level handler deleted, the exception now escapes `run_command_gate` entirely. Concrete case: a long gate run with `on_tick` = lease renewal, where a transient renewal failure raises `OSError`/`ConnectionResetError` after the command has started. Under the old code the gate degraded to `("unavailable", {"reason": "could not execute: ..."})`; with this diff the exception propagates out of `run_command_gate` (there is no `p.could_not_run` flag set for it), so a lease-renewal blip aborts gate evaluation instead of yielding an `unavailable` result. The fix for finding #1 only relocates where the callback error goes; it does not answer that `run_command_gate` lost the handler that used to contain it.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/runner.py (`run_command_gate`, the `p = P.run_shell(...)` call)

chunk_findings.detail: This file lives under `tests/guard_baselines/` and, like `subprocess_calls.toml`/`complexity_d_or_worse.toml`, is a ratchet baseline: the guard compares the actual state against the recorded set and fails when they differ ("the failure message prints the exact value"). The change's stated scope is that `proc.run_shell` replaces `gates._run_ticking`, `run_command_gate`, `ci`, `bisect`, `review` and the private `killpg` copies. The edit removes `ddflow.services.ci` and `ddflow.services.gates.runner` (consistent with that scope) but it *also* removes `ddflow.services.onboard_tests`, a module the change does not claim to touch, while *retaining* `ddflow.services.bisect` and `ddflow.services.review`, which the change does claim to convert. Concretely: if `ddflow.services.onboard_tests` still has its `subprocess` import (as it does not appear anywhere in the described conversion), the recorded baseline no longer contains that `module -> subprocess` pair while the actual import set still does, so the import-linter guard fails on the missing allowance; conversely, if `bisect`/`review` were fully converted, the retained entries fail it the other way. The two asymmetries (converted module kept, unconverted module dropped) cannot both be right, and the fix is to reconcile this baseline with the actual post-change set of `subprocess` importers rather than editing entries that the stated change neither adds nor removes.
chunk_findings.title: tests/guard_baselines/importlinter-subprocess-home.toml (removed line `"ddflow.services.onboard_tests -> subprocess"`)

chunk_findings.detail: The fix for the earlier tick-callback finding only guards the `except (OSError, ValueError)` branch with `if from_tick: raise`; the preceding `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch does not consult `from_tick` at all. `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` is a `SubprocessError`, i.e. not an `OSError`/`ValueError`, so if the caller-supplied `on_tick` callback raises it (a very natural thing for a lease-renewal callback that shells out to a CLI or otherwise uses `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)`), `tick()` records it in `from_tick` and re-raises, it propagates out of `_shell_group`, and `run_shell` catches it here and returns `ShellResult(None, _text(exc.output), _text(exc.stderr), timed_out=True, ...)`. The caller is then told the *operator's command* timed out and was killed, when in fact the command may still be running normally and only the callback's own subprocess timed out — the same "attribute the callback's trouble to the command" defect that finding #1 was about, just through the other handler. The `if from_tick: raise` guard needs to be present in the `TimeoutExpired` branch as well (before returning the timed-out result).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/proc.py:run_shell (`except subprocess.TimeoutExpired as exc:` branch)

chunk_findings.detail: The old body wrapped the run in `try: ... except subprocess.TimeoutExpired ... except (OSError, ValueError) as exc: return "unavailable", {"reason": f"could not execute: {exc}", ...}`. The new body has no `except` at all: it assumes `run_shell` never raises and instead reports every failure through `p.timed_out` / `p.could_not_run`. But `run_shell` is invoked with `on_tick=on_tick` and runs that callback *on this thread* (that is the whole point of the ticking path). Prior finding #1 was confirmed precisely because a `ValueError`/`OSError` raised by `on_tick` was being swallowed into `could_not_run=False`; the fix for it stops `run_shell` from mislabeling such an error, which means the error is no longer contained inside `run_shell` either. With the gate-level handler deleted, the exception now escapes `run_command_gate` entirely. Concrete case: a long gate run with `on_tick` = lease renewal, where a transient renewal failure raises `OSError`/`ConnectionResetError` after the command has started. Under the old code the gate degraded to `("unavailable", {"reason": "could not execute: ..."})`; with this diff the exception propagates out of `run_command_gate` (there is no `p.could_not_run` flag set for it), so a lease-renewal blip aborts gate evaluation instead of yielding an `unavailable` result. The fix for finding #1 only relocates where the callback error goes; it does not answer that `run_command_gate` lost the handler that used to contain it.

chunk_findings.detail: This file lives under `tests/guard_baselines/` and, like `subprocess_calls.toml`/`complexity_d_or_worse.toml`, is a ratchet baseline: the guard compares the actual state against the recorded set and fails when they differ ("the failure message prints the exact value"). The change's stated scope is that `proc.run_shell` replaces `gates._run_ticking`, `run_command_gate`, `ci`, `bisect`, `review` and the private `killpg` copies. The edit removes `ddflow.services.ci` and `ddflow.services.gates.runner` (consistent with that scope) but it *also* removes `ddflow.services.onboard_tests`, a module the change does not claim to touch, while *retaining* `ddflow.services.bisect` and `ddflow.services.review`, which the change does claim to convert. Concretely: if `ddflow.services.onboard_tests` still has its `subprocess` import (as it does not appear anywhere in the described conversion), the recorded baseline no longer contains that `module -> subprocess` pair while the actual import set still does, so the import-linter guard fails on the missing allowance; conversely, if `bisect`/`review` were fully converted, the retained entries fail it the other way. The two asymmetries (converted module kept, unconverted module dropped) cannot both be right, and the fix is to reconcile this baseline with the actual post-change set of `subprocess` importers rather than editing entries that the stated change neither adds nor removes.

chunk_findings.detail:
The old code extracted the resolved MERGE_HEAD with `head.stdout.strip()`, but the new code passes `head.out` straight into the second git call:

```python
head = G.run(".", "rev-parse", "-q", "--verify", "MERGE_HEAD", timeout=G.PROBE_TIMEOUT)
merging = head.ok and (
    G.run(".", "merge-base", "--is-ancestor", head.out, "HEAD", timeout=G.PROBE_TIMEOUT).code
    != 0
)
```

`G.run` returns a raw `GitResult` whose `.out` is the decoded stdout/`err` text (that is why the sibling sites in this same diff still need `paths()`/slicing to post-process it, e.g. `docscheck._tree`'s `r.paths()` and `r.err[:200]`). If `.out` carries the trailing newline that `git rev-parse` emits (`"<40-hex>\n"`), then `merge-base --is-ancestor "<40-hex>\n" HEAD` is given a 41-char object name. Git cannot parse `"<sha>\n"` as a revision (it is neither a 40-char hex oid nor a valid ref name), so the command fails with a non-zero/128 exit even though MERGE_HEAD *is* an ancestor of HEAD.

Concrete failure: a stale or planted `MERGE_HEAD` that points at HEAD (the exact rubber-duck case the comment says this code was written to reject). Old behaviour: `merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` exits 0 → `merging` is False → the trailer rule still applies. New behaviour: the trailing newline makes `merge-base` exit non-zero while `head.ok` is True, so `merging` becomes True, the ordinary commit is treated as an in-progress merge, and the trailer rule is bypassed again — reintroducing the exemption the change claims to fix. Either `head.out.strip()` is required, or the wrapper must guarantee `.out` is already trimmed (the container hunks that dropped `.strip()` only survive because `bool("x\n")` happens to still be True, so they do not demonstrate that `.out` is stripped).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/setup.py (the `head = G.run(".", "rev-parse", ...)` / `merge-base` block, ~line 530)

chunk_findings.detail: The old call was `P.run(["git", "-C", str(repo), "ls-files", "-z", "--cached"], capture_output=True, timeout=60)`; the replacement `G.git_paths(repo, "ls-files", "--cached")` passes no timeout at all, while the two sibling conversions in the same file deliberately carry their timeouts forward (`_grep` keeps `timeout=120`, `staged_diff` keeps `timeout=120`). So this is the only one of the three sites whose run is no longer bounded. Input that demonstrates it: a `repo` whose `git ls-files` blocks — an index on a stale NFS/SMB mount, a `.git` that triggers a credential or fsmonitor helper, or a huge tree on a slow disk. Previously `_tracked_tokens` returned `None` (the "cannot determine tokens" signal that makes the docsync check skip) after 60 s; now the call blocks indefinitely and the whole docsync pass hangs, with no timeout on the `git_paths` invocation to stop it. The asymmetry within the same diff (120 s retained twice, the 60 s removed once) is what makes this a regression rather than an intended default.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/docsync.py `_tracked_tokens`

chunk_findings.detail:
The old body was `out = (r.stdout or "").strip(); return out if r.returncode == 0 and out else None`, i.e. it always handed callers a whitespace-trimmed string. The new body returns `r.out` verbatim. `infra.git.run` is the low-level argv wrapper: its `.out` is the raw captured stdout — the very value the old code had to call `.strip()` on — and every successful git command terminates stdout with a newline. So given a repo whose `git config --get remote.origin.url` prints `https://example.com/x.git
`, `_git` now returns `"https://example.com/x.git
"` instead of `"https://example.com/x.git"`. That value is fed into this module's `urlparse`/`url2pathname` path handling and into comparisons against the resolved `root`, so the parsed local path becomes `.../x.git
` and the install-kind/source classification is corrupted. The `.strip()` (or an equivalent trim) needs to be restored; the type annotation `str | None` hides the fact that the returned string is no longer normalized.

chunk_findings.detail: The old single-file baseline `tests/guard_baselines/write_text.toml` recorded `baseline = 10` for the guard `write_text`. The intent states the replacement must preserve the same counts ("Behaviour of the guards is identical (same counts, same messages)", "The total is derived"). Summing the newly added per-module entries gives 1 (`ddflow.api.setup`) + 1 (`ddflow.infra.harness_identity`) + 2 (`ddflow.services.gates.mutation`) + 1 (`ddflow.services.gates.runner`) + 2 (`ddflow.services.sessions`) + 1 (`ddflow.services.shared_files`) = **8**, not 10. So either two `write_text` sites have been dropped from the ratchet (if the guard only checks modules that have an entry file, those two call sites are now silently unguarded), or the guard will now fail on the two sites that live in modules with no entry (if a missing module file is treated as 0). In neither case is the behaviour identical to the old baseline, and the guard's own ratchet invariant (`baseline` must never be raised / must match actual site count) is violated by the migration itself. The two missing sites need to be located and their modules given the correct entry so the derived total returns to 10.

chunk_findings.detail: The new baseline files are named after full module paths (e.g., `ddflow.surfaces.commands.knowledge.toml`) and each contains a bare `baseline = N` value, but the stated intent is to split the baseline into one file per top-level package (`api`, `services`, `infra`, `core`, `surfaces`, `views`) with per-module counts inside. If the guard loads `tests/guard_baselines/complexity_d_or_worse/<top-level-package>.toml` and looks up the module key—as the intent describes—these per-module files will never be read. For example, running the guard on `ddflow.surfaces.commands.knowledge` (which has 2 complexity D-or-worse sites per the new file) would find no entry for it (or no `surfaces.toml`), so the guard would treat the baseline as zero and fail, demanding the author raise the baseline or fix the code. This breaks the guard’s behavior instead of preserving it.

If the six listed modules are the only ones that contain `Path.write_text` sites (which is what the split claims), then two counts have been dropped relative to the previous baseline, so "behaviour of the guards is identical (same counts)" is not true. Concretely: if a module that actually has write_text sites is absent from this directory, the guard now sees it as baseline 0 (missing entry) and either fails on existing sites that the old total of 10 permitted, or — if the guard only iterates over present entries — silently stops ratcheting on those two sites. Either outcome differs from the old single-total behaviour. (Caveat: if the remaining two counts live in per-module files added outside this diff part, this is not a defect.)

chunk_findings.detail: The `below` branch special-cases `count == 0` with `f"now delete {path} in this same change, so the sites cannot grow back."`, where `path = _module_baseline_path(kind, module).relative_to(ROOT)`. Per the stated design this baseline is "a directory with one small file per top-level package (api, services, infra, core, surfaces, views)" keyed by *full module name* (the earlier finding enumerated modules such as `ddflow.services.gates.mutation`, `ddflow.services.gates.runner`, and `ddflow.services.sessions`, all of which live in the same top-level package `services`). So `_module_baseline_path` must map several distinct modules onto one shared package file (e.g. `tests/guard_baselines/write_text/services.toml`). Concrete failure: suppose `ddflow.services.gates.mutation` goes from 2 sites to 0 while `ddflow.services.gates.runner` still has 1 site and `ddflow.services.sessions` still has 2. The guard emits, for `mutation`, "now delete tests/guard_baselines/write_text/services.toml in this same change". An author who follows that instruction deletes the file and thereby drops the `runner`/`sessions` entries; the next run then reports those modules with `baseline = 0` in `above` and the guard fails on previously-clean modules. The remediation text is wrong: for a package file shared by sibling modules it must say to remove that module's entry, not to delete the file (the old single-file guard had no delete variant at all, so this special case is newly introduced).

chunk_findings.detail: The deleted total baseline recorded `baseline = 19`, and the ratchet contract in that same file states the baseline is kept in sync with the code ("Lower the baseline in the same change that removes sites"), which is also why the other guards in this diff sum exactly (`git_argv`: 4 = `ddflow.infra.log` 2 + `ddflow.services.importer` 2; `hashlib`/`os_replace` are 0 and are deleted). This diff removes the `subprocess_calls` total but only adds four per-module files: `ddflow.infra.forge.toml` = 1, `ddflow.infra.log.toml` = 2, `ddflow.infra.paths.toml` = 1, `ddflow.infra.signals.toml` = 1 — a derived total of 5, not 19. Fourteen counted sites (anything outside the excluded `ddflow.infra.proc`/`ddflow.infra.git`, e.g. the `services`/`api` modules that the other guards in this same series cover) therefore have no per-module entry. Under the per-module lookup the change describes, those modules either resolve to a default of 0 (so the guard now fails on sites it previously allowed) or are no longer matched at all (so the sites are silently unenforced); either way the behavior is not "identical" and the effective total shifted from 19 to 5 without any site being removed. No site removal or guard-code change appears in this diff to justify the drop.

chunk_findings.detail:
The assertion that gives this test its name can never execute. In

```python
with s.hold(0) as slot, pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3):
    assert slot.index == 0
```

the body of a `with` statement runs only after *every* context manager's `__enter__` has returned. `s.try_hold(-3)` raises `SlotsTimeout` from `__enter__` (that is exactly what `pytest.raises` was put there to swallow), so control jumps to `pytest.raises.__exit__`, which returns `True`; `s.hold(0).__exit__` is then called with `(None, None, None)` and the statement completes. The body — `assert slot.index == 0` — is never reached, on any input.

Consequence: nothing in the file verifies the "clamp a sub-1 limit to 1" behaviour at all. An implementation where `Slots.hold(0)` clamps the *limit* to 1 for the blocking check but hands out an arbitrary index (say 5, or index 0 of a differently-sized pool), or where the limit is clamped to any value ≥ 1, still passes this test. The only thing the test actually pins down is that `hold(0)` does not itself raise; the claim in the test name is unasserted. The likely intended shape is

```python
with s.hold(0) as slot:
    assert slot.index == 0
    with pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3):
        pass
```

which puts the assertion in a body that runs.

(Everything else in the file — the fake-clock timeout assertion `ft.now >= 103`, the empty-sleep check for a zero timeout, the lowering/raising-limit cases, and the flock subprocess kill case — checks a condition that a wrong implementation would actually violate, so there is nothing to report there.)

In `with s.hold(0) as slot, pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3):`, the third context manager is entered before the block body; `s.try_hold(-3)` raises `SlotsTimeout` from its `__enter__`, so control jumps straight out of the `with` statement (the body is skipped) and `pytest.raises` suppresses the exception. The assertion needs to sit in its own block, e.g. `with s.hold(0) as slot: assert slot.index == 0` followed by a separate `with pytest.raises(SlotsTimeout), s.try_hold(-3): pass`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The added/deleted detection (`new file mode` / `deleted file mode`) is only run in the `seen` branch, i.e. only when a `---`/`+++`/rename line was found. But a *newly added empty file* (and any added/deleted binary file) has no `---`/`+++` lines at all, so control takes the early return and `_from_header_line` sets both sides to the same path. Concretely, `git diff --cached` after `touch empty && git add empty` produces:

```
diff --git a/empty b/empty
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..e69de29
```

`parse_section` returns `FileDiff(head, "empty", "empty")`, contradicting the dataclass contract "old ... None for an added file". The same happens for a file deleted to empty, and for every binary add/delete (`Binary files /dev/null and b/x differ`, no `---`/`+++`): e.g. a deleted binary gets `new == "x"` where it should be `None`. Any consumer using `f.old is None`/`f.new is None` (rather than `path`) to decide add vs delete vs rename misclassifies these files.

chunk_findings.detail:
The fallback that fires when a section has no `---`/`+++`/rename lines only splits the header into two paths for the symmetric `a/X b/X` / `X X` case; otherwise it returns the entire remainder as `new`, `None` as `old`. That is reachable with an asymetrically named binary file, e.g. `git diff --no-index --binary a/old.bin b/new.bin` emits

```
diff --git a/old.bin b/new.bin
index ...
Binary files a/old.bin and b/new.bin differ
```

Here `pair = "a/old.bin b/new.bin"`, `pair[9] == " "` so `left="a/old.bin"`, `right="b/new.bin"`; the prefixes match but `left[2:] != right[2:]`, so the function falls through to `return None, "a/old.bin b/new.bin"`. `FileDiff.path`/`paths`/`touched_paths` then report the bogus string `"a/old.bin b/new.bin"` and lose both real paths (compared against a coverage set, neither `old.bin` nor `new.bin` matches). The same happens for `diff.noprefix` when a path literally begins with `a/` or `b/` (the symmetric check `pair[half] == " "` lands on the wrong offset).

chunk_findings.detail:
`FileDiff.old`/`new` are documented as "None for an added file" / "None for a deleted file", and the `seen` branch carefully computes `added`/`deleted` from the `new file mode` / `deleted file mode` lines. But when a section has no `---`/`+++`/`rename` line — exactly the empty-file and binary-file cases the module docstring calls out — the function returns early and never applies that logic. Input:
```
diff --git a/logo.png b/logo.png
new file mode 100644
index 0000000..1234567
Binary files /dev/null and b/logo.png differ
```
`_from_header_line("a/logo.png b/logo.png")` sees the symmetric split (`left[2:] == right[2:]`) and returns `("logo.png", "logo.png")`, so `parse_section` yields `FileDiff(old="logo.png", new="logo.png")` for a file that was *added*. The same happens for an added/deleted empty file (`new file mode 100644` + `index 0000000..e69de29`, no hunks) and for the quoted-name variant `diff --git "a/café" "b/café"` (len(quoted)==2). Any consumer that distinguishes added/deleted/modified via `f.old is None` / `f.new is None` (the documented contract) silently mislabels every newly added image/binary/empty file as a modification, and deleted binaries as modifications too. Applying the existing `added`/`deleted` scan in this branch would fix it without affecting the genuine mode-change case (`old mode`/`new mode` lines don't start with `new file mode`, so a mode-only section still yields `old == new == path`).

chunk_findings.detail:
`header_path` unquotes and then strips `a/`/`b/`, assuming the prefix is present. `_from_header_line` explicitly accommodates `diff.noprefix` output (`if left == right: return left, left`), but the `---`/`+++` path does not, so under `diff.noprefix=true` a file whose real path begins with `b/` is corrupted. Input (with `-c diff.noprefix=true`):
```
diff --git b/logo.png b/logo.png
index 1111111..2222222 100644
--- b/logo.png
+++ b/logo.png
@@ -1 +1 @@
-old
+new
```
`old = header_path("--- b/logo.png", "a/") = "b/logo.png"` (correct) but `new = header_path("+++ b/logo.png", "b/") = "logo.png"` (wrong), so `FileDiff` reports a spurious rename and `touched_paths` yields `{"b/logo.png", "logo.png"}`, inventing a path that does not exist (a file named `a/...` fails symmetrically). The same diff without `noprefix` handles `a/b/logo.png` correctly, so the two code paths disagree about the same repo state.

chunk_findings.detail: The fallback comparison is lossy: `os.fsencode(p).decode("utf-8", "replace")` replaces *every* invalid byte with U+FFFD, and the new comment states the diff side is decoded the same way, so any two paths that differ only in non-UTF-8 bytes collapse to the same value. Concretely, with `core.quotepath` at its default and two changed non-UTF-8 files, say `a\xe9` and `a\x80`, `git status -z` keeps them distinct (they arrive as surrogate-escaped strings, as the comment says), so `changed` holds both. If the diff silently drops `a\x80` and shows only `a\xe9`, `unidiff.touched_paths(diff)` yields `{"a\ufffd"}`. For `p = "a\x80"` the exact check `p not in shown` is true, but the fallback maps it to the identical `"a\ufffd"`, so it is judged present and the function returns `(True, [])` — the exact "silent omission" of a changed file that this guard exists to catch goes unreported. The removed `_c_quoted` matched the distinct octal spellings git actually emits (`a\200` vs `a\351`), so the default `core.quotepath=true` case was previously collision-free; this change reintroduces the collision for every repo, not just `quotepath=false` ones.

A header-only section with two *different* names still cannot be split, and the old side is silently discarded. Concretely, `git diff --no-index --binary old.bin new.bin` emits:

chunk_findings.detail: This re-raises prior finding 3, which is *not* answered for the input that actually reaches the lossy branch. The probe (`test_two_non_utf8_names_are_not_confused_when_the_diff_drops_one`) only exercises the default `core.quotepath=true` case, where git C-quotes the diff header and `unidiff` unquotes the octal back to a UTF-8+surrogateescape string (`a/\351` -> `a\udce9`), so the *exact* check `p not in shown` already works and the fallback never fires. The fallback fires only when the diff side held a *raw* non-UTF-8 byte, i.e. `core.quotepath=false`: the change's own comment says `_diff_text` decodes the diff with `errors="replace"`, so a raw `\xe9`/`\x80` byte becomes U+FFFD there, while the status side (read with `-z`, which ignores `quotepath`) keeps the bytes as surrogate escapes. Concretely: with `git config core.quotepath=false`, two changed files named `a\xe9` and `a\x80`, and a diff (from `capture_diff`, which pins only `--src-prefix`/`--dst-prefix`, not `quotepath`) that contains only `a\xe9`: `changed` holds both distinct surrogate strings, `unidiff.touched_paths` yields `{"a\ufffd"}`, and for `a\x80` the first test (`"a\udc80" not in shown`) is true but the second, `os.fsencode("a\udc80").decode("utf-8","replace")` -> `"a\ufffd"`, *is* in `shown`, so the dropped file is silently reported as present. The guard therefore fails closed-open exactly on the case it exists to catch, whenever two changed names differ only in invalid UTF-8 bytes. A byte-level comparison (compare `os.fsencode(p)` against the raw header bytes, or pin `core.quotepath`) would be needed; a UTF-8 `errors="replace"` round-trip cannot distinguish these names.

chunk_findings.detail: The cache treats `(st_size, st_mtime_ns)` as a content identity: if the signature is unchanged it returns the previously stored hash without re-reading. That is only sound when mtime actually changes on every content change, which is false whenever the filesystem's mtime resolution is coarser than the interval between two writes, or when a writer preserves mtime. Concretely: hash `a.txt` containing `"x"` (size 1, mtime T), then rewrite it with `"y"` (still size 1) within the same timestamp tick — on vfat/exFAT (2 s granularity), or on ext4/NTFS/network mounts where the kernel's coarse clock can hand two quick writes the same `st_mtime_ns`, and with any tool that restores mtime (e.g. an archive extraction or `cp -p`). The next `scan()` finds `cached[0] == (1, T)`, sets `value = cached[1]`, and returns the hash of `"x"`. `changes(old)` then produces an empty `Changes`, so `ChangeDetector` reports "nothing changed" for a file whose content actually differs — a false negative in the one operation the module exists to perform. The docstring frames this as an optimization, but it converts a "detect drift" contract into a "detect drift except for same-size edits within one mtime tick" contract, and nothing in the API surfaces that limitation to callers.

chunk_findings.detail: `test_a_file_whose_stat_is_unchanged_is_not_read_again` locks in the behaviour that a file is only (re-)hashed when its `(size, mtime)` stat pair has moved — the second `scan()` must perform *zero* reads (`assert counting.reads == []`, line 58). Since `changes()` compares the new manifest against the old one and the new manifest is produced by that same stat-gated scan, a modification is reported as `unchanged` whenever the stat pair is identical, even though the bytes differ. Concrete input: a file rewritten in place with different content of the *same byte length* while the mtime does not advance — which is exactly what happens (a) on filesystems with 1-second timestamp granularity (HFS+, ext3, many NFS/FUSE/overlayfs mounts) when two writes land in the same tick, and (b) whenever mtimes are preserved/restored (`git checkout`/`git stash pop` of a same-size file, `cp -p`, `tar -xp`, `rsync --times`). In those cases `det.changes(old_manifest)` returns `modified == ()`, so the worker skips a file that really changed. `test_a_same_size_rewrite_is_noticed_when_its_mtime_moves` (lines 61-70) deliberately pushes the mtime 5 s into the future before asserting detection, i.e. it only passes because the failing condition is engineered away; the suite therefore never covers the same-size / same-mtime edit that the cache silently swallows.

chunk_findings.detail: `PRUNE = (".git",)` is applied only to entries in `os.walk`'s `dirs`, i.e. it only skips directories. In two common environments `.git` is a *regular file* in the working tree: every submodule working directory contains a `.git` file (`gitdir: …`), and a linked worktree created with `git worktree add` has a `.git` file at its root. Because `scan()` calls `candidates()` with `self.patterns` defaulted to `()` and the module's own contract is "An empty set matches everything", `matches(".git", ())` returns `True`, the `exclude` set is empty, `lstat` succeeds (mode is `S_ISREG`), and `.git` is hashed into the manifest. So `ChangeDetector(root=Path(worktree_or_submodule)).scan()` (or any pattern set broad enough to match it, e.g. `("**",)`) returns `{".git": "<hash of 'gitdir: …'>", …}` — git's own metadata reported as project content, directly contradicting the comment "git's own, never part of a work tree's content". The failure is observable, not just cosmetic: a worktree's `.git` file holds an absolute gitdir path, so relocating the checkout or re-cloning a submodule changes that file's bytes, and the next `changes()` call reports a `modified` entry for a path that is not part of the tree's content and that no consumer glob (`docs/**`, skill/subagent globs) would ever want.

chunk_findings.detail:
The documented guarantee is "A file that is there but cannot be read is neither removed nor modified: it keeps the hash it last had" (module docstring, and `_last`'s comment "path -> the last hash taken ... what an unreadable file keeps"). That fallback reads only the in-process `_last` cache; it never consults the `old` manifest that `changes(old)` is handed, even though the class doc says "The manifest is plain data the caller keeps wherever it keeps state." So when the manifest is persisted and the detector is constructed fresh for the next run — exactly the usage the API invites, since `changes` takes `old` as a parameter rather than storing it — an existing-but-unreadable file is dropped from the new manifest and reported as `removed`.

Concrete input: a previous run stored `{"a.txt": H}`. New process, `d = ChangeDetector(root); d.changes({"a.txt": H})`. `a.txt` still exists but is unreadable (mode 000, or read denied). `candidates()` lists it, `lstat()` succeeds, it is `S_ISREG`, the re-hash returns `None`, `self.unreadable` gets `"a.txt"`, and `value = self._last.get("a.txt")` is `None` because the cache starts empty. `value is None` so the path is not added to `manifest`, and `diff(old, manifest)` returns `a.txt` in `Changes.removed` — contradicting the stated "neither removed nor modified" contract. The same false `removed` occurs with a reused detector whenever the passed `old` differs from `_last` (e.g. a manifest from two scans ago). The fallback needs the caller's `old` (or `scan` needs to be given it), not just the volatile `_last`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring promises "committed after it, **staged**, unstaged and untracked", but the only index-aware command used would be `git diff <commit>`, and that command is defined as *working tree* vs `<commit>`, not *index* vs `<commit>` (the index-vs-commit form is `--cached`/`--staged`, which is not used here). The second listing, `ls-files --others --exclude-standard`, only supplies *untracked, non-ignored* paths. Therefore any difference that lives only in the index is invisible:

- Input: repo at commit `sha` where `foo` = `A`; `echo B > foo; git add foo; echo A > foo`. `git status --short` reports `M  foo` (staged), but `git diff --name-only --no-renames sha` compares worktree `A` against `sha` `A` and prints nothing, and `ls-files --others --exclude-standard` prints nothing (the path is tracked in the index), so `changed_since(root, sha)` returns `[]` — "nothing changed" for a staged change.
- More practically: `git rm --cached cfg.local` where `cfg.local` is in `.gitignore` (tracked in `sha`, deleted from the index, still on disk with unchanged content, now ignored). `git diff sha` sees worktree content identical to `sha`, `ls-files --others --exclude-standard` suppresses it as ignored, so the staged deletion is never reported, again contradicting the documented "staged" coverage and the module's rule that "could not tell" is never "nothing changed".

Adding `G.git_paths(root, "diff", "--cached", "--name-only", "--no-renames", sha)` (and unioning it with the existing listings) would close the gap.

chunk_findings.detail: In the old code the only reference to `signal.SIGKILL` was inside the `if os.name == "posix":` branch, so on a non-POSIX host (`os.name == "nt"`) the name was never evaluated and `import ddflow.infra.proc` succeeded; the module deliberately supports non-POSIX hosts (that is exactly why the `os.name == "posix"` guard and the `p.kill()` fallback exist). In the new code `signal.SIGKILL` is a *default argument*, and default arguments are evaluated once at function-definition time, i.e. at module import. On Windows `signal` defines only `SIGABRT`, `SIGBREAK`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGILL`, `SIGINT`, `SIGSEGV`, `SIGTERM` — `SIGKILL` is documented as Unix-only and raises `AttributeError`. So `import ddflow.infra.proc` (and therefore `infra/log.py`, which now imports and uses it heavily) fails at import on Windows, a regression the branch-only reference did not have. A concrete fix is to resolve the default lazily/module-level, e.g. `_SIGKILL = getattr(signal, "SIGKILL", signal.SIGTERM)` and use `sig: int = _SIGKILL`, or default `sig: int | None = None` and normalize inside the posix branch.

chunk_findings.detail: `_stop` delegates both kills to `P.kill_group` but no longer states either of the two behaviours the previous code encoded explicitly: the hard-kill signal and the error suppression. The old body was `os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL)` wrapped in `contextlib.suppress(ProcessLookupError, PermissionError)`; the new body is a bare `P.kill_group(proc)`, and the first call likewise drops the `suppress`. The docstring still promises "SIGKILL to the group *unconditionally*". Concretely: for a server that ignores SIGTERM (the `npx`/grandchild case the docstring names), `_stop` sends SIGTERM, waits 3 s, then calls `P.kill_group(proc)` — if `infra.proc.kill_group`'s default signal is anything other than SIGKILL (e.g. SIGTERM, or it re-sends whatever was last used), the grandchild survives and the "unconditional SIGKILL" promise is broken while a leaked process tree remains. And for a server whose group has already vanished because it exited/crashed on its own before `_stop` ran, `os.killpg` inside `kill_group` raises `ProcessLookupError`; the removed `contextlib.suppress(ProcessLookupError, PermissionError)` used to swallow this, so unless `kill_group` suppresses it, the very first line of `_stop` now raises, `_await_exit` and `proc.wait` never execute, and the leader is left unreaped. Both behaviours are now implicit in an unshown helper, whereas the code being replaced made them explicit.

chunk_findings.detail:
The test name and the intent (`companions._stop uses proc.kill_group` precisely to reap a whole process tree) promise coverage of the *whole group*, but the only assertion is `p.wait(timeout=10) == code` on the group **leader**. The child is `sh -c "sleep 60 & wait"`, so the real target of the group kill is the grandchild. An implementation of `kill_group` that signals only its argument — e.g. `kill_group(p, sig=None)` implemented as `p.send_signal(sig or SIGKILL)` instead of `os.killpg(os.getpgid(p.pid), ...)` — kills the `sh` leader with exactly the requested signal and returns `-15` / `-9`, so both parametrizations still pass, while the `sleep 60` grandchild survives and is reparented. That is the exact leak `_stop` needs to prevent. Demonstration: replace `P.kill_group(p, sig)` with `p.send_signal(sig)`; `test_kill_group_sends_the_chosen_signal_to_the_whole_group` stays green for both `(None, -SIGKILL)` and `(SIGTERM, -SIGTERM)`. To actually cover the stated property, the test would need to observe the grandchild (e.g. capture its pid and assert it is gone, or assert no process in the group remains) rather than only the leader's exit status.

I deliberately do not report the POSIX shell's exit-status-on-SIGTERM behaviour or the deleted baselines, because I cannot establish a concrete failure for either from the material available.

chunk_findings.detail: In the old code the only reference to `signal.SIGKILL` was inside the `if os.name == "posix":` branch, so on a non-POSIX host (`os.name == "nt"`) the name was never evaluated and `import ddflow.infra.proc` succeeded; the module deliberately supports non-POSIX hosts (that is exactly why the `os.name == "posix"` guard and the `p.kill()` fallback exist). In the new code `signal.SIGKILL` is a *default argument*, and default arguments are evaluated once at function-definition time, i.e. at module import. On Windows `signal` defines only `SIGABRT`, `SIGBREAK`, `SIGFPE`, `SIGILL`, `SIGINT`, `SIGSEGV`, `SIGTERM` — `SIGKILL` is documented as Unix-only and raises `AttributeError`. So `import ddflow.infra.proc` (and therefore `infra/log.py`, which now imports and uses it heavily) fails at import on Windows, a regression the branch-only reference did not have. A concrete fix is to resolve the default lazily/module-level, e.g. `_SIGKILL = getattr(signal, "SIGKILL", signal.SIGTERM)` and use `sig: int = _SIGKILL`, or default `sig: int | None = None` and normalize inside the posix branch.

chunk_findings.detail: `_stop` delegates both kills to `P.kill_group` but no longer states either of the two behaviours the previous code encoded explicitly: the hard-kill signal and the error suppression. The old body was `os.killpg(proc.pid, signal.SIGKILL)` wrapped in `contextlib.suppress(ProcessLookupError, PermissionError)`; the new body is a bare `P.kill_group(proc)`, and the first call likewise drops the `suppress`. The docstring still promises "SIGKILL to the group *unconditionally*". Concretely: for a server that ignores SIGTERM (the `npx`/grandchild case the docstring names), `_stop` sends SIGTERM, waits 3 s, then calls `P.kill_group(proc)` — if `infra.proc.kill_group`'s default signal is anything other than SIGKILL (e.g. SIGTERM, or it re-sends whatever was last used), the grandchild survives and the "unconditional SIGKILL" promise is broken while a leaked process tree remains. And for a server whose group has already vanished because it exited/crashed on its own before `_stop` ran, `os.killpg` inside `kill_group` raises `ProcessLookupError`; the removed `contextlib.suppress(ProcessLookupError, PermissionError)` used to swallow this, so unless `kill_group` suppresses it, the very first line of `_stop` now raises, `_await_exit` and `proc.wait` never execute, and the leader is left unreaped. Both behaviours are now implicit in an unshown helper, whereas the code being replaced made them explicit.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/companions.py:_stop

chunk_findings.detail:
The test name and the intent (`companions._stop uses proc.kill_group` precisely to reap a whole process tree) promise coverage of the *whole group*, but the only assertion is `p.wait(timeout=10) == code` on the group **leader**. The child is `sh -c "sleep 60 & wait"`, so the real target of the group kill is the grandchild. An implementation of `kill_group` that signals only its argument — e.g. `kill_group(p, sig=None)` implemented as `p.send_signal(sig or SIGKILL)` instead of `os.killpg(os.getpgid(p.pid), ...)` — kills the `sh` leader with exactly the requested signal and returns `-15` / `-9`, so both parametrizations still pass, while the `sleep 60` grandchild survives and is reparented. That is the exact leak `_stop` needs to prevent. Demonstration: replace `P.kill_group(p, sig)` with `p.send_signal(sig)`; `test_kill_group_sends_the_chosen_signal_to_the_whole_group` stays green for both `(None, -SIGKILL)` and `(SIGTERM, -SIGTERM)`. To actually cover the stated property, the test would need to observe the grandchild (e.g. capture its pid and assert it is gone, or assert no process in the group remains) rather than only the leader's exit status.

I deliberately do not report the POSIX shell's exit-status-on-SIGTERM behaviour or the deleted baselines, because I cannot establish a concrete failure for either from the material available.

chunk_findings.detail: The new parameter is documented as "SIGKILL when None, SIGTERM to ask it to stop first", and the fallback keys off `sig is None`, but the POSIX kill keys off truthiness: `os.killpg(p.pid, sig or signal.SIGKILL)`. The two predicates disagree for real `sig` values, which produces two wrong outcomes. (1) `kill_group(p, sig=0)`: signal 0 is the POSIX "send nothing, just test the group" probe, but `0 or signal.SIGKILL` evaluates to SIGKILL, so the whole group is hard-killed — a destructive action where the caller asked for a no-op/existence check. (2) `kill_group(p, sig=signal.SIGKILL)`: on the main path the group correctly gets SIGKILL, but if `os.killpg` raises `ProcessLookupError`/`PermissionError` and control reaches the fallback, `sig is None` is False and the direct child gets `p.terminate()` (SIGTERM), not SIGKILL — so for the same documented meaning ("SIGKILL"), passing `None` and passing `signal.SIGKILL` behave differently, and a child that ignores SIGTERM can survive a call that explicitly requested SIGKILL. Writing both predicates as `signal.SIGKILL if sig is None else sig` / `if sig is None` (or, if 0 must stay meaningful, testing `sig is None` uniformly) makes them agree.

chunk_findings.detail: The new signal parameter uses falsiness to default to SIGKILL, which is not the same as the documented "SIGKILL when None". `sig: int | None` admits `0`, which is the standard POSIX liveness probe (`kill(pgid, 0)` checks existence/permission without delivering a signal); given `kill_group(p, 0)`, `0 or signal.SIGKILL` evaluates to `signal.SIGKILL`, so the call silently **kills** the whole process group the caller only asked to probe. Any other falsy int would be substituted the same way. The function's own fallback a few lines below gets this right with `if sig is None: p.kill() else: p.terminate()`, so the POSIX branch should likewise test `sig is None` (e.g. `signal.SIGKILL if sig is None else sig`) rather than rely on truthiness. No in-tree caller passes `0` today, hence LOW, but the parameter is a general-purpose entry point and the expression contradicts its stated contract.
