chunk_findings.detail: `default_was` is declared `Any = None` and is never required when `default_changed_in` is set, unlike the sibling paired metadata just below (`choices` without `strictest` raises `ValueError`). A section module that declares, say, `knob(default=5, doc="...", default_changed_in="1.5")` and omits `default_was` is accepted silently, and the doc string that `config --explain` renders becomes `... (Default changed in 1.5; it was None.)` — asserting the previous default was `None`, which is false for a knob whose default is 5. Because `None` doubles as both the "unset" sentinel and a legitimate previous default, the code cannot tell a half-specified declaration from a real "the old default was `None`" declaration, so any consumer that keys off `default_was` (the D-upgrade-config-changes confirmation the intent says this metadata drives) either compares against the wrong value or skips the confirmation. Either raise when `default_changed_in` is set and `default_was` was not supplied, or use a distinct sentinel (e.g. `MISSING`) so the omission is detectable.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/_docs.py `knob()` (`if default_changed_in:` block, `default_was` field)

chunk_findings.detail: `skipped_fields` decides which fields a table entry "does not have" by comparing the raw TOML keys to `cls.__dataclass_fields__`, i.e. to the entry dataclass's *attribute names*. The loaders it is supposed to mirror do not use that notion of "known": this change adds knob metadata `renamed_from` that is "applied at load", so an older key is consumed by the migration and the entry is *not* skipped at all. Because `skipped_fields` re-parses the file with `tomllib` and never consults the knob metadata, any key that a field accepts via `renamed_from` (nor, for the same reason, any other accepted alias) is reported as an extra field. Concretely: for an entry class whose field `new` carries `renamed_from="old"`, loading a config containing `[table.<id>]` with `old = ...` migrates the value into `new` with no skip, yet `skipped_fields` computes `set(raw) - known` and emits `("[table.<id>] in <path>", ["old"])`; `ddflow doctor` then lists `old` as a skipped/unknown field written by a newer ddflow, and an operator following that advice will delete a key that this version actually honours. The probe for the previous finding on `enforce.py` (`_waivers_members`) does not address this, since it is about malformed waiver entries, not about the `known`-set used for the skipped-field report.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/tomlcfg.py::skipped_fields (`known = set(cls.__dataclass_fields__)`)

chunk_findings.detail:
The change description defines a single `upgrade_advice(highest, install)` — the one function that "replaces the 3 copies of `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X`" and that is supposed to make the remedy "fit how this ddflow is installed" (source tree → merge main, otherwise the install-method upgrade command). In `report`, the newly added call site invokes it with neither argument:

```python
def advice() -> str:
    nonlocal fix
    fix = fix or II.upgrade_advice()
    return fix
```

Given the stated two-parameter signature, this is an arity error. It fires on exactly the paths this file was added to serve: as soon as `cfg.unknown_knobs` is non-empty, `skipped_table_fields()` yields a row, or `cfg.file_format > CONFIG_FORMAT`, the f-strings call `advice()` and `doctor` raises `TypeError: upgrade_advice() missing 2 required positional arguments: 'highest' and 'install'` instead of printing the advice. Even if the target function happens to have defaults, passing no `highest` means the emitted remedy can never name the version to upgrade to, so it no longer does what `upgrade_advice(highest, install)` is defined to do. (Cross-checking the described API against its call sites is the only way to see this, since the function body lives outside this diff.)
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configcompat.py:51 (`report.advice`)

chunk_findings.detail: `RENAMED` maps an old spelling of a knob to its current spelling (the change's own knob metadata is `renamed_from`, i.e. a single alternate name per key, so `RENAMED[old]` is the new dotted name as a string). Indexing it with `[0]` therefore takes the *first character* of the current spelling rather than the spelling itself. Concretely, for a renamed key like `lease.duration_s` whose current name is `lease.ttl_s`, setting it (`config --set lease.duration_s 30`) makes `_written_keys` return `{"l"}` instead of `{"lease.ttl_s"}`. The caller then runs `Config.check(result, written={"l"})`; per the method's contract a written key this version does not know must raise, and `l` is not a dotted path in `data`, so the edit is refused with a bogus "unknown key" error, i.e. every write of a renamed key fails (and the value that was actually written is never the one judged). The docstring itself says the result must be "each under its CURRENT spelling", which `RENAMED[k][0]` does not produce. If `RENAMED` really is old→new string (as the metadata implies), the expression should be `RENAMED[k]`.

chunk_findings.detail: The single advice helper introduced by this change is `upgrade_advice(highest, install)` (stated in the survey as replacing the three `"Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X"` copies); `install_info` merely re-exports the same objects (`running_from_source`/`is_source_tree` are the same object per the prior triage). Calling `II.upgrade_advice()` with zero arguments therefore does not satisfy that signature: given a file whose declaration is newer than this code (`format = N`, N > `CONFIG_FORMAT`), `format_problem` reaches this line and raises `TypeError: upgrade_advice() missing 2 required positional arguments` (or, if a defaulted wrapper exists, produces advice with no required version, e.g. `to >= None`). The intended behaviour is a clean exit-3 refusal carrying fitted upgrade advice; instead the writer crashes out of `config --set` / `append_block` for exactly the input this function was added to handle (a newer-format config).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/configwrite.py::format_problem (`advice = II.upgrade_advice()`)

chunk_findings.detail: This change replaces the old, total expression `str(ddflow.__version__)` with a bare `running_version()` in the two export paths, while the *same* change, in `install_info.py::own_distribution`, deliberately writes `V.running() or "unknown"`. That `or "unknown"` is only meaningful if `core.version.running()` can return a falsy value (None/""), which is exactly why it is there. The export callers drop that guard, so in an environment where the running version cannot be determined — no distribution metadata and no `ddflow.__version__` fallback (e.g. a source checkout that was never `pip install`ed / a vendored bundle) — `version` is left as `None` and is passed straight into `frame("", k.name, version, extra)` (registry.py) and into the frame built by `write.py`. The producing-version stamped into the exported artifact then reads `None` (or trips frame's own validation) instead of the `"unknown"` that the sibling reader in `install_info.py` is careful to produce. The two new call sites need the same `or "unknown"` (or a shared helper that guarantees a non-empty str) as `own_distribution` got; otherwise the reader's contract is violated in the very paths it was introduced for.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/export/registry.py (version = running_version(), ~line 575) and ddflow/services/export/write.py (version = running_version(), ~line 392)

chunk_findings.detail:
The test's name and docstring claim it verifies two behaviours — that a malformed `enforce.trailer_waivers` entry is *refused when written* and *only noted when it sits in a file* ("The tolerance is for what a FILE holds") — but the body only exercises the write path:

```python
for bad in ('{ "Phase-ships" = "none" }', '{ "Phase-ships" = ["none", 5] }'):
    err, _ = _set(_repo(tmp_path, ""), "enforce.trailer_waivers", bad)
    assert isinstance(err, CW.KeyRefused) and "enforce.trailer_waivers" in err
```

`_set` is `CW._write_config`, so every assertion is about `--set`; no `Config.load` of a file containing `[enforce.trailer_waivers]\nPhase-ships = "none"` is performed and `cfg.ignored_members` is never inspected. This matters because the test is the cited probe for the earlier finding that `_waivers_members` cannot distinguish a newer release's shape from a plain malformed entry (anything `_waivers_problem` rejects is reclassified as an unknown member and dropped from the table the check sees, e.g. `[enforce.trailer_waivers]\nPhase-ships = "none"\n` loads as an empty/unknown table). The probe shows only that the *write* path is strict; it never demonstrates that a malformed value already present in a file is "noted" rather than silently discarded (or, conversely, that it does not brick the load). Because that specific file-content claim is untested, the earlier finding is not actually refuted by this probe — either a silent-drop regression or a brick-on-load regression of a malformed file waiver would let this test pass.

chunk_findings.detail: The change's own contract is "upgrade advice that fits how ddflow is installed" / "otherwise the upgrade command for the install method", and `upgrade_advice` is documented as `upgrade_advice(highest, install)` — i.e. it is parameterised by the actual install method, the same information `doctor` is made to consult via `install_info`. Here the non‑source branch instead hardcodes `kind="index"` and never consults the real install method. Concrete environment: ddflow installed by `pipx`/`uv` (anything whose kind is not `index`), config contains a key this version skips; the stderr line then tells the user to run the index/pip upgrade command, which does not upgrade that installation (and disagrees with what `doctor` prints for the same install). Ahead of this change the line named no command at all, so this is a new, actively misleading instruction rather than an unchanged behaviour. Note also that because `is_source_tree()` short‑circuits and the test suite runs from a source checkout, the `else` branch is never executed in tests, so the call's argument list is not exercised: if `upgrade_advice`'s second parameter is `install` rather than `kind` (as the intent text states), this line is a `TypeError` that only fires for exactly the non‑source installs the feature is meant to serve.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_routers_members` classifies every entry by shape (`isinstance(m, list) and all(isinstance(x, str) for x in m)`) and, for every entry that fails, substitutes `[]` *before* the knob's own validation runs. That subsumes the guard the knob is documented to have: the comment kept immediately above this knob says the check exists precisely because "a string where a list belongs (`hydrafusion = "openai"`) would iterate as letters: a set of nonsense". Given a config file containing

```toml
[agent]
routers = { hydrafusion = "openai" }
```

(or `hydrafusion = [1, 2]`, or any other non-list-of-words value) the old load/`ddflow_configure` path rejected the file with the actionable "must be a list of words" problem; with this change the helper turns the entry into `{hydrafusion: []}` first, `ok`/`check` therefore sees a well-formed list of strings, and no error is ever raised. The only trace is a stderr note ("router 'hydrafusion' (a shape not known here, so its families are unknown)"), and the user's mistyped family list is discarded in memory (and in any file this version rewrites): the router silently becomes "unknown families", so `complete --model hydrafusion` refuses later with a version-mismatch story instead of the config error that named the actual mistake. This is also inconsistent with its sibling in the same change: `_kinds_members` explicitly leaves a value that "is not a list of words" alone and says so in its docstring ("A value that is not a list of words is left to the check") — i.e. members-normalisation feeds the check, so the two helpers should agree on which inputs the check is still allowed to reject. If the goal is only to neutralise *newer-release shapes* (a dict such as `{ families = [...] }`), a malformed scalar/list-of-non-strings should be passed through unchanged so the existing shape check still fires, exactly as the kinds helper does.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/agent.py (`_routers_members`, the `members=` hook on `agent.routers`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new branch asserts the source-tree remedy with a capital `M`, but the sibling test added for the same change, `test_doctor_names_every_skipped_field_ignored_member_and_newer_format` in tests/test_compat_config.py (prior finding 8, triaged `confirmed`, whose probe is that same test), asserts the lowercase `"merge main" in out` against the same `doctor` output. Doctor prints this remedy exactly once, so at most one of those two positive assertions can hold; the change cannot be green in both environments. The concrete failure: on a source checkout or editable install — `II.install_info().kind in ("source-tree", "editable")`, which is precisely the dev/CI-editable case this branch is written for — this test takes the first branch and line `assert "Merge main" in out` evaluates to False, because the emitted remedy is the lowercase `merge main` string that the pre-existing assertion in this same file (`assert "merge main" not in out`, and the finding-8 test) is written against. The runner then fails even though the advice was correctly install-aware. Either the capital `M` here is wrong, or the lowercase assertion in finding 8's test is wrong and that finding's fix is incomplete; the two assertions must be aligned to the actual emitted string.

data.body:
Research R-compat, decision D-compat (operator 2026-10-06). Today the skew guard keys only on __version__. A branch or source tree that adds kinds without a bump, every patch release, and unpinned MCP entries slip through. Add a ddflow.capabilities event: the first write that uses a capability records it, like git's repository format extensions. A writer then checks the capabilities a write needs against the ones it has. Examples: minting an id under a configured template it cannot render, writing a rule while rules are events, appending under a redaction profile it lacks. Only that write is refused (D-compat 2), with the version that provides the capability; everything else proceeds. Dedupe and definition digests are computed on normalized text (whitespace, case, and redaction markers mapped to one token), so clones on different redaction profiles reach the same match. The skew guard also compares FORMAT_LEVEL. Tests: an older capability set against a newer log, for each capability.

Widened 2026-10-06 (unification survey): every digest input is serialised through core.events.canonical (core.digest.of_obj). Separate sorted dumps exist at services/triggers.py:88/258 (no separators, so they disagree with canonical), flowstate.py:317/321, quota.py:266 and bugreport.py:456. Stored trigger definitions keep a legacy digest mode so existing digests still match.

Unification survey 2026-10-06: Note: output_digest uses two algorithms for one field (content_digest 16 at api/review.py:552, blake2b-8 at api/gates.py:674) and they are compared at progress.py:143; B-uni-tree-identity unifies it, and compatibility keeps old values comparable.

Split into: B-uni-compat-capabilities.1-format, B-uni-compat-capabilities.2-capabilities, B-uni-compat-capabilities.3-digests.

chunk_findings.detail: The override filter compares the recorded `log_format` against a value that depends on the *current* running `format_level`, not against the log's format. Concretely: the log has a `ddflow.seen` stamp at version "2.0" carrying `format_level: 2`; the running ddflow is version "1.0" with `FORMAT_LEVEL = 1`. Here `version_skewed` and `format_skewed` are both true, so the user's override is written with `log_version: "2.0"`, `log_format: 2`. Now the ddflow is upgraded to `FORMAT_LEVEL = 2` (same version "1.0", same log, `highest_format` still 2). `format_skewed` becomes `2 > 2 == False`, so this line demands `log_format == 0`, the recorded `2 != 0`, `override` stays `None`, and the writer is refused again (exit 3) because `version_skewed` is still true — even though the log state is exactly the state the override was recorded for and the format has not advanced ("covers that format only" should still hold). The condition should compare against `highest_format` unconditionally (the log's format), since any dependency on the *reader's* `format_level` lets a ddflow upgrade silently invalidate an existing override. The same defect is hard-coded in the `format_level is None` path, where `format_skewed` is always false, so any override that recorded a non-zero `log_format` is never recognized by callers that omit `format_level`.

The new format branch is documented (in its own comment) as the case where the log's FORMAT is ahead while the writer has "the same or a newer version number". But the shared footer still reads `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= {highest}`. In this branch `facts.highest` is the highest *version* stamp, which by construction is `<= version` (the running version is "the same or newer"), so that instruction is already satisfied and retrying after following it changes nothing — the same `SkewRefused` is raised again.

Concrete input: log's filename stamp `highest = "2.0.0"`, `highest_format = 3`, running `version = "2.0.0"` (or `"2.1.0"`), `fmt = 2`. `skew_message` takes the format branch (`3 > 2 > 0`) and emits `... Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 2.0.0 and retry ...`. The user is already on `>= 2.0.0`, so the prescribed remedy is a no-op; the log is permanently un-writable unless they upgrade to a build that writes format level `>= 3` (which need not be `highest`, since format and version are allowed to diverge) or use the override. The message should name the required *format level* / a version that writes it, not reuse the version-based `>= {highest}` advice. Note the version-older sub-case of the same branch happens to be correct, which masks the defect.

chunk_findings.detail: The format branch asserts `this project's log has been worked on by ddflow {highest}{who} at data format level {log_format}`, where `who`/`highest` derive from `facts.highest_by`/`facts.highest` (max *version*) while `log_format` is `facts.highest_format` (max *format*). Since this feature explicitly permits version and format to diverge, these can come from different stamps. Input: agent X at version `3.0` stamps `format_level = 1`, agent Y at version `2.0` stamps `format_level = 5`; then `highest = 3.0`, `highest_by = X`, `highest_format = 5`, and the message claims "ddflow 3.0 (stamped by X) at data format level 5", attributing to X a format level it never wrote. Only a message, but the fact it states is false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/infra/log.py skew_message (format branch attribution)

chunk_findings.detail: The test asserts `not facts.format_skewed` for `stamp_facts(_events(("0.3.0", 3)), "me", "0.2.0", 2)`, even though the log’s highest format level (3) is greater than the writer’s (2). This makes the flag false precisely when the log’s on-disk format is ahead, contradicting the intent that a writer at a lower format level than the log’s highest stamp is refused. Combined with the override logic, the test `test_a_version_override_carries_no_format_and_a_format_skew_needs_its_own` expects a version-only override to carry no `log_format`. Given a log stamp with version 99.0.0 and format `FORMAT_LEVEL + 1`, calling `override_skew` for the version would then record no format, so the subsequent `append` would be allowed despite the log format being higher. The test should assert `facts.format_skewed` is true (or not assert false) so the override can cover the format.

chunk_findings.detail: The extra event is constructed with `subject="d"` rather than `subject="ddflow"`; every other `ddflow.seen` event in this file uses `subject="ddflow"`. If `stamp_facts` filters to the expected subject (as the domain implies), this malformed event is skipped before its `format_level: True` is examined, so the assertion `highest_format == 0` passes even when `True` is mistakenly treated as level 1. The test therefore does not verify that boolean format levels are ignored.

chunk_findings.detail: The test name claims to cover equal or lower formats, but it only writes a stamp at `ddflow.FORMAT_LEVEL` (equal). A stamp at `ddflow.FORMAT_LEVEL - 1` is never tested, so a regression that treats a log’s lower format as skew would not be caught.

titles: ddflow/core/events.py:255 (`stamp_facts`, override match `d.get("log_format", 0) == (highest_format if format_skewed else 0)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The override matcher requires `log_format == highest_format` using the *raw* local flag (true whenever `highest_format > format_level`, even when the version is also behind), but the only value `stamp_facts` exposes to the code that writes the override is `StampFacts.format_skewed`, which is forced to `False` in exactly that both-behind case. Concretely: log has `ddflow.seen(version="2.0", format_level=3)`, this agent runs `version="1.0"` with `FORMAT_LEVEL=2`; then `highest_format=3`, `version_skewed=True`, and reported `format_skewed=False`. An override recorded from the reported facts carries `log_format=0` (the "format it covers", as reported), while the matcher demands `log_format == 3`, so `override` stays `None` and the process exits 3 on every subsequent run even though the user overrode — contradicting "the override (skew.overridden) records log_format and covers that format only". The complementary case fails the same way if the writer instead records `facts.highest_format` unconditionally: `version="1.0"` + `FORMAT_LEVEL=2` against a stamp `version="2.0", format_level=1` stores `log_format=1` (`highest_format>0`, `format_skewed=False`, so `version_skewed` alone makes `skewed=True`), while the matcher then demands `log_format == 0`. Either way the override written for a skew that is still present is discarded and the refusal repeats.

chunk_findings.detail: In the format-specific branch (`log_format > format_level > 0`), the shared tail still says `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= {highest}`. This branch is explicitly for the case where the log’s format is ahead but the writer’s version is **not** older (the code comment says “the same or a newer version number, an older data format”). For example, with `version="6.0"`, `highest="5.0"`, `log_format=5`, and `format_level=3`, the condition is true, and the function returns a message ending with `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 5.0 and retry ...`. The caller is already on 6.0, which satisfies `>= 5.0`, so the advised remediation is impossible and does not address the refusal, which is caused solely by the older format level. The message should instead tell the user to obtain a ddflow that writes format level `>= log_format`.

chunk_findings.detail: `assert log.read_all()[-1].data["older_ddflow"] == ddflow.__version__` assumes the event appended by the local clone is the last element returned by `read_all()`. But the test first calls `_stamp(...)`, which writes a `future.jsonl` shard containing `ts="2099-01-01T00:00:00.000000Z"` and `lamport=1`. If `EventLog.read_all()` orders merged events by timestamp (or by `(lamport, ts)`), that 2099 stamp is the last event, not the local append, and its `data` dict has no `older_ddflow` key. The assertion then raises `KeyError` instead of checking the override. The helper deliberately uses a far-future timestamp, so any timestamp-based or timestamp-tie-broken merge ordering makes this test fail spuriously.

chunk_findings.detail: The event intended to exercise an invalid `format_level: True` is constructed with `subject="d"`: `Event(kind="ddflow.seen", subject="d", data={"version": "0.2.0", "format_level": True})`. Every other `ddflow.seen` stamp in this file uses `subject="ddflow"` (`_events` and `_stamp`). chunk_findings.detail:
`format_skewed` is documented in the same diff as "Only the format level is behind: the running version is not older than the log's highest stamp". The computation does not enforce that: it is `format_level is not None and highest_format > format_level`, with no reference to `highest`/`version`.

Input: stamps `{"version": "3.0", "format_level": 1}` by agent X and `{"version": "2.0", "format_level": 5}` by agent Y; running `version = "1.0"`, `format_level = 2`. Then `highest = "3.0"` (the running version *is* older), `highest_format = 5`, `format_version = "2.0"`, `format_by = "Y"`, and `format_skewed` is `True`. A consumer that selects the format-ahead branch on `format_skewed` (which is the only thing that flag exists for, and whose premise per its own comment is "the same or newer version number") will take that branch for a log that is in fact version-skewed. The message then names the format carrier (Y/2.0) and tells the user to upgrade to `>= 2.0`, which does not clear the version skew (the real requirement is `>= 3.0`); following the advice leads to another `SkewRefused`. The confirmed fix for finding #2 changed the footer text but not the condition, and its probe (`...the_format_only_message...`) exercises only the format-only case, so it does not cover this both-skewed input.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `format_version`/`format_by` fields are documented as "The version and agent of the stamp that carries `highest_format` ("" when none does)". The selection `(level, version_key(v), v) > (highest_format, version_key(format_version), format_version)` has no guard that `level >= 1`, so a stamp that carries no format (level taken as `0` by `_format_of`) still wins the tie-break on version and sets these fields. Since the existing `highest` selection already relies on `version_key("")` sorting below any real version, `(0, version_key(v), v) > (0, version_key(""), "")` is true for any non-empty `v`.

Input: `stamp_facts([Event(kind="ddflow.seen", agent="me", data={"version": "1.0"})], "me", "1.0", 1)` — no stamp carries `format_level`. `highest_format` stays `0` and `format_skewed` is `False`, but `format_version` becomes `"1.0"` and `format_by` becomes `"me"`, contradicting the documented "" when no stamp carries a format. Any consumer that reads these attributes to describe the log's format (the purpose the fields were added for, per the fix for finding #3) will name a stamp that carries no format level. The comparison needs a `level >= 1` (or equivalent) precondition.

chunk_findings.detail:
The `format_only` branch is entered only when `format_only and log_format > format_level > 0`. When `format_only` is true but the local writer's `format_level` is `0` (the "unknown/undeclared format" state that the sibling guard in the `else` branch — `if log_format > format_level > 0` — was clearly added to handle, and the default of the parameter itself), the function silently falls into the version-based `else` branch. That branch emits `"...this ddflow is {version}, which is older"` and the remedy `"Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= {highest}"`, both of which are wrong precisely in the case this feature targets: a writer whose *version* is not older, only its data format.

Concretely: the log contains `ddflow.seen(version="5.0", format_level=5)`, the local agent runs `version="6.0"` with `FORMAT_LEVEL=0`. Then `format_only` is true (format 5 > 0, and 6.0 is not older than 5.0), `log_format=5`, `format_level=0`. The guard `5 > 0 > 0` is false, so the message returned is `"REFUSED: ... worked on by ddflow 5.0, and this ddflow is 6.0, which is older ... Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 5.0 and retry"`. The agent is told it is *older* than 5.0 (it is not) and told to upgrade to a version it already exceeds, so the "fix" is a no-op and the format skew is never explained. This is the same class of defect that the previous review's finding #2 raised and that the new `format_only` branch was added to fix, but the extra `format_level > 0` conjunct leaves that sub-case uncovered; the condition should key on `format_only` (the value already encodes that the version is not older), not re-derive the skew from `log_format > format_level > 0`.

chunk_findings.detail: `Capability.kinds` is documented ("The event kinds a write of which uses it") and consumed as a set of *event kinds*: `capabilities_used` does `kind in CAPABILITIES[n].kinds` and `capability_gap` does `kind in rec.kinds`, where `kind` is an event kind such as `"bug.found"` / `"session.started"`. The argument passed instead is `_redact.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS`, i.e. the set of text *fields* the log redaction profile rewrites (the module is the redaction profile; its constant is named `..._FIELDS`). No event kind is ever a member of that set, so for every kind `kind`, `CAP_LOG_REDACTION in capabilities_used(kind, active)` is false: no `ddflow.capabilities` event is ever written for it, and `capability_gap` never returns it. Given any write (e.g. `bug.found` with free text), a writer that lacks the full log-redaction profile is therefore not refused, exactly the guard this change is supposed to add. Contrast the sibling `CAP_ID_TEMPLATE` entry, which enumerates concrete event kinds — the redaction entry needs the same kind-level set (the kinds whose data carries log text), not the field-name set.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py — `CAP_LOG_REDACTION` entry in `CAPABILITIES` (`frozenset(_redact.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS)`)

chunk_findings.detail: The new function annotates a parameter with `Iterable[str]`, but the module's import block does not import `Iterable`: the hunk shows `from typing import Any`, then `from . import clock`, the added `from . import redact as _redact`, `from .digest import content_digest`, and then `SCHEMA_VERSION = 1` — no `Iterable` (and the change adds none). Annotations on a `def` are evaluated when the statement executes unless `from __future__ import annotations` is in effect, so `import ddflow.core.events` raises `NameError: name 'Iterable' is not defined` and every consumer of the module fails to import. The addition of `from . import redact as _redact` in this same import block shows this is where such an import would belong.

chunk_findings.detail:
The docstring promises "the result does not depend on the order the shards are read in", but the recorded agent is order-dependent whenever two capability events tie on version. Concretely, if shard A contains `{capability: "X", kinds: [...], version: "1.0.0", agent: "alice"}` and shard B contains the same capability/version with `agent: "bob"`, then:

- read order A→B: `old = RecordedCapability(..., "1.0.0", "alice")`; `newer` is `False` (equal tuples), so `by` stays `"alice"`.
- read order B→A: `old.by` is `"bob"`, so `by` ends as `"bob"`.

Both orders produce the same version and kinds union but a different `by`, contradicting the stated order-independence and making the recorded provenance (and any refusal/message derived from it) non-reproducible for identical log contents. The `_h_ddflow_capabilities` handler folds the same event set and does not have this property (it keeps all agents), so the two "same way" folds also disagree on the tie case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/events.py `_fold_capability` (the `newer = (version_key(v), v) > (version_key(old.version), old.version)` line)

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `capability`, `kinds`, and `version` to the redaction profile for `ddflow.capabilities`, but omits the recorder identity. The new `capabilities` field in `ddflow/core/records.py:915` documents exactly what a `ddflow.capabilities` record carries: `{"kinds" (sorted), "version" ..., "agents", "at"}`. So the event data includes an `agents` entry (the agents that recorded the capability). The redaction map is a per-`(kind, field)` replacement map — fields without an entry are passed through unchanged (note that only a subset of each kind's fields is listed, e.g. `("ddflow.seen", "format_level")`, so it is clearly not an allow-list of everything to show, and `at` is exempt by the same convention). Consequently, redacting/displaying a tail of a log that contains a `ddflow.capabilities` event prints the raw agent identities verbatim, while comparable identities elsewhere are masked (`("def.merged", "source"): "an origin id or path"`, `("decision.recorded", "item"): "an item id"`). Concretely: a log whose first capability record was written by user/agent `[REDACTED:email]` (recorded as `agents: ["[REDACTED:email]"]`) yields an unredacted `agents` value in the redacted tail, leaking the recording identity the profile is meant to hide. An entry such as `("ddflow.capabilities", "agents"): "agent names"` is missing.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/redact.py:536-538 (new `ddflow.capabilities` entries)

chunk_findings.detail: The filter `if e.kind != "ddflow.capabilities"` removes capability events from the ordered list before asserting `order[:2] == ["ddflow.seen", "phase.added"]`. This means the test no longer verifies the ordering of the capability record relative to the upgrade stamp, even though the capability event is itself produced by the same first write the test is about. Concretely: if the implementation were changed to emit `ddflow.capabilities` before `ddflow.seen` (i.e. the stamp does not precede the event that caused it), the log would read `["ddflow.capabilities", "ddflow.seen", "phase.added", ...]`, the filter would drop the capability event, and the assertion would still pass. The test's own comment ("The stamp precedes the event that caused it") states the property that this filter now silently exempts capability events from; a regression in capability-vs-stamp ordering would go undetected.

chunk_findings.detail: `Capability.kinds` is declared (and every consumer treats it) as a set of *event kinds*: `capabilities_used(kind, active)` tests `kind in CAPABILITIES[n].kinds` with `kind` an event kind, and `capability_gap`/`capability_unrecorded` compare event kinds against `rec.kinds`. The `CAP_LOG_REDACTION` capability is built with `frozenset(_redact.LOG_TEXT_FIELDS)`. As the constant's own name and the surrounding "full `log` redaction profile" comment indicate, `LOG_TEXT_FIELDS` is the set of *payload field names* the profile redacts (e.g. `summary`, `text`, `note`), not event kinds. Given any real write, e.g. `capabilities_used("bug.found", {"log-redaction-full"})`, the membership test is `"bug.found" in {"summary", "text", ...}` which is `False`, so the capability is never reported as used, is never recorded by the first write that uses it, and `capability_gap` can never refuse a writer that lacks it (`kind in rec.kinds` likewise compares an event kind to field names). The log-redaction capability is therefore inert, defeating the half of the stated intent ("the log redaction profile register the first capabilities"); only `CAP_ID_TEMPLATE`, whose kinds really are event kinds, behaves as intended.

chunk_findings.detail: `_MARKER = re.compile(r"\[REDACTED(?::[a-z0-9_]*)?\]?")` does not require a marker to be well-formed: the closing `]` is optional and the `:<kind>` part only accepts `[a-z0-9_]`, so the pattern happily matches the bare prefix `[REDACTED` of strings that are not markers. Given the input `print('[REDACTEDX]')`, `normalize_markers` matches `[REDACTED` (the kind group is skipped because `X` isn't `:`, and `\]?` is skipped because the next char is `X`), substitutes `[REDACTED]`, and returns `print('[REDACTED]X]')` — corrupted non-marker text rather than the input unchanged. The same root cause mangles any marker whose kind uses a character outside `[a-z0-9_]` / any non-lowercase spelling: `normalize_markers("[REDACTED:API_KEY]")` matches only `[REDACTED:` (the `*` quantifier matches empty at the uppercase `A`, and `\]?` fails) and yields `[REDACTED]API_KEY]` instead of the unified `[REDACTED]`. Because these strings are the inputs to dedupe/definition digests, such text is silently rewritten into a different value before hashing, so the digest no longer reflects the stored content; the comment's claim that the pattern covers "a redaction marker in any spelling" is not met by the character class and the optional delimiter.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/digest.py:33 (`_MARKER` / `normalize_markers`)

chunk_findings.detail: The change's stated contract is that *both* the dedupe digest and the definition digest are "computed on normalized text (whitespace, case, redaction markers to one token)". This test asserts the opposite for definitions: `DEFS.digest({"cmd": "make"}) != DEFS.digest({"cmd": "Make"})` and `DEFS.digest({"cmd": "a b"}) != DEFS.digest({"cmd": "a  b"})`. Concretely, if `DEFS.digest` routes its input through the same canonicalization/normalization that `D.normalized` applies in `test_normalized_reaches_every_string_and_nothing_else` (which folds case and collapses whitespace) before calling `D.of_obj`/`content_digest`, then `{"cmd": "make"}` and `{"cmd": "Make"}` hash to the same canonical string and the first assertion fails; `{"cmd": "a b"}` and `{"cmd": "a  b"}` collide the same way and the second fails. Conversely, if the implementation intentionally keeps case/whitespace significant for definition digests, then the change does not deliver the "one canonical form" it claims for definitions: two definitions that differ only in case or spacing will be reported as changed rather than matched. Either the two `!=` assertions are wrong (they contradict the change's own normalization goal and will fail against the intended implementation) or the definition-digest normalization advertised in the intent is not actually implemented, so this needs to be reconciled.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_compat_digests.py :: test_a_definition_digest_still_sees_case_and_whitespace

chunk_findings.detail: The marker pattern `r"\[REDACTED(?::[a-z0-9_]*)?\]?"` makes the closing bracket optional (`\]?`) and lets the kind body be empty (`*`), so it does not match "the `[REDACTED:<kind>]` … and the bare `[REDACTED]`" as its own comment claims; it matches any occurrence of the bare prefix `[REDACTED`, including text that is not a redaction marker at all. Two consequences. (1) Over-normalization / false equality: the string `"a[REDACTED"` and the string `"a[REDACTED]"` both normalize to `"a[REDACTED]"`, so records whose canonical text differs only by the presence of the bracket collapse to one dedupe/definition digest. (2) Under-normalization of real markers: because the kind class is `[a-z0-9_]`, a marker spelled with any other character stops matching right after the colon and leaves residue — `"[REDACTED:API_KEY]"` becomes `"[REDACTED]API_KEY]"`, not `"[REDACTED]"`, so a clone produced with a kind-style profile (e.g. `[REDACTED:API_KEY]`) will not match the masking profile's `[REDACTED]`, which is exactly the clone equality this change is supposed to guarantee. A pattern anchored to a complete marker (`r"\[REDACTED(?::[a-z0-9_]+)?\]"`) would satisfy both halves of the stated intent.

chunk_findings.detail: The change replaces every hard-pinned remedy string (`"Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 99.0.0"`, `"Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 0.3.0"`, `"Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= 9.9.9"`) with an assertion whose expected value is produced by the very function under test: `upgrade_remedy` is imported from `ddflow.infra.log` and its output is checked for containment in the message that `skew_message` (also in `ddflow.infra.log`) builds from that same helper. This makes the assertions tautological with respect to the wording the intent says must stay pinned ("keeping the REFUSED / --allow-older-version wording the tests and docs pin"). Concretely, if `upgrade_remedy` is ever changed or broken to return `""`, then `"" in str(exc.value)` is `True` for every string, so `test_...` at the 99.0.0 case, `test_a_version_skew_that_is_also_a_format_skew_says_both` (0.3.0), and the 9.9.9 case all pass while the emitted message contains no remedy text at all — the exact regression these tests exist to catch. Likewise, any drift in the literal `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X` prefix (e.g. dropping the version, changing the binary name) is invisible because both sides of the comparison move together. To actually pin the wording the expected value must be a literal string, not `upgrade_remedy(...)`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test claims to pin the new promise ("running_version delegates to core.version.running"), but it only asserts `LOG.running_version() == ddflow.__version__` after monkeypatching `ddflow.__version__` — which is exactly what `core.version.running` is supposed to read, and exactly what the *old* implementation (`return ddflow.__version__`) read. The test therefore cannot distinguish the delegating implementation from a direct self-read: revert `log.running_version` to `return ddflow.__version__`, or make `core.version.running` start normalizing/deriving the version (e.g. stripping a `+dirty`/local suffix), and this test stays green while the stated behaviour regresses. To actually observe delegation it must monkeypatch the delegate itself (`ddflow.core.version.running`, i.e. `core.version.running`), not the shared underlying attribute.

chunk_findings.detail: `_unrecorded` hardcodes the message "the rule file was written but not recorded in the log", but it is a shared helper called from two paths with opposite effects on the file. `_retire_in_log` calls it when a removal succeeded on disk but the log could not be updated (e.g. `def_retire` hits a lock timeout, or returns a non-OK exit such as a skew-guard refusal, hitting `return _unrecorded(outcome, res.reason)`). In that case the file was *deleted*, not written, so the user is told "the rule file was written" while the rule is actually gone and the log still holds a live definition. Input: `rule.remove` successfully deletes the file and `def_retire` fails; the resulting outcome's `data["unrecorded"]` asserts the file was written, sending the operator (and any recovery/migration logic keyed off that text) to look for a file that no longer exists and to distrust the removal that did happen.

chunk_findings.detail: The test's name and docstring promise it verifies that `findings` now "reads a shared glob the way `core.globs` does", but the only assertion tied to the actual change is `assert not hasattr(schedule, "_gitattributes_re")`. The behavioural assertion is not sensitive to the change: before the slice, `schedule._gitattributes_re` was itself a re-export of the very same compiled regex from `core.globs`, so `findings(Path("/nonexistent-repo"), cfg)` with `["a[z-a]"]` produced the identical `"...cannot be read as git reads it"` problem when `shared_files.py` imported it via `schedule._gitattributes_re`. Concrete scenario: a follow-up replaces the `from ddflow.core.globs import ...` import in `shared_files.py` with a private copy of the same regex (`_GIT_GLOB_RE`). The shim stays deleted, `findings` still flags `a[z-a]` with the same text, and this test still passes — even though `shared_files.py` no longer reads globs through `core.globs`, which is the coupling the slice exists to guarantee. Only a check that the symbol `findings` actually uses is `core.globs`'s object (e.g. asserting `SF.<regex_name> is core.globs.<regex_name>`, or deleting/patching the `core.globs` symbol and observing the change) would catch that regression.

chunk_findings.detail:
`_protected` drops a lease with `if iid == ignore: continue`, and `dispose_tree` passes `ignore=item.id if item else ""`. The exemption is therefore keyed to the *item*, not to the actor that actually holds the lease, even though the code has the holder in hand (`lease.holder`, already used to build `who`). The docstring justifies this with an assumption — "``item``'s own lease -- the caller holds it -- does not count" — that the implementation does not enforce.

Concrete interleaving: process A takes a live lease on item X and starts working on X's tree T. Process B, working from a survey that predates A's lease (the exact TOCTOU the guard exists for), calls `dispose_tree(repo, cfg, log, T_worktree, item=X)`. The guard is supposed to see A's live lease on T and return `Disposal("refused", ..., "held")`. Instead `iid == "X" == ignore`, so the lease is skipped, `W.remove` succeeds, and T is deleted out from under A (and `forced_by` makes it a forced removal if B passes it). The guard's stated purpose — "a tree a LIVE lease holds ... is refused" — is bypassed for any item handed to the function.

The same hole opens for the logging mode the function advertises: because a passed `item` also selects `record_item_removed` instead of the path-wide `record_removed`, a cleanup/onboarding caller that passes the owner item merely to get the tidier log entry silently loses the lease protection for a tree that is still in use. Exempting the lease by the *holder that is making the call* (e.g. compare `lease.holder`/a caller token with `ignore`) rather than by `item.id` would close it; as written, the exemption and the protection are conflated.

chunk_findings.detail: The change lowers the ratchet baseline from 2 to 1, but the file's own contract says to delete the file at zero. This is only correct if this same change removes exactly one D-or-worse complexity site in `ddflow.services.cleanup`. If `dispose_tree` was refactored but the net number of D-or-worse complexity sites in that module is unchanged (e.g., the new `dispose_tree` itself lands at complexity D or worse, offsetting whatever was removed), the guard would now fail on the next run because the recorded baseline understates the real count. However, this diff is a fragment of a 6-part change and the actual post-change complexity count cannot be verified from the data given here, so I cannot demonstrate a concrete input that makes it wrong.

chunk_findings.detail:
The scan only recognises two alias-qualified call spellings, `W.remove(` and `worktree.remove(`:

```python
if p.name != "worktree.py" and re.search(r"\bW\.remove\(|worktree\.remove\(", p.read_text())
```

A fifth removal path that imports the function directly does not contain either pattern, so the assertion `callers == ["services/cleanup.py"]` still passes while an unguarded, unlogged removal exists. Concretely: add `ddflow/services/release.py` containing `from ddflow.infra.worktree import remove` and a call `remove(wt)`; `remove(wt)` matches neither alternative (the import line contains `worktree import remove`, not `worktree.remove(`), the file is therefore not in `callers`, and the test that is meant to prove "nothing but `cleanup.dispose_tree` removes a worktree" goes green. The same blind spot covers `infra_worktree.remove(...)` or any other alias, i.e. exactly the "new caller of `worktree.remove`" the docstring claims would be caught. (The check should also match the bare `remove(`/imported name, or better, assert on the worktree module's own call sites rather than on string spellings in callers.)
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_tree_dispose.py:test_nothing_but_dispose_removes_a_worktree

chunk_findings.detail:
The whole point of `dispose_tree` (as its own docstring states) is "one guarded, logged removal under the log lock", serialised with the claims: the guard re-reads leases under `log.transaction()` and `W.remove` runs inside that transaction. But the branch-ref removal is dedented *outside* the transaction:

```python
with log.transaction() if log else contextlib.nullcontext():
    ...
    r = W.remove(repo, cfg, wt, force=bool(forced_by))
    ...
if had_branch and W.branch_exists(root, wt.branch):
    rb = W.git(root, "branch", "-d", wt.branch)
```

So the branch is deleted after the lock is released, with no re-check of leases/claims at the moment of the delete. Concrete interleaving: `dispose_tree` disposes the worktree for branch `feature/x` (guard passes, `had_branch=True`), the `with` exits and the lock is released; before the `if had_branch` line runs, another actor (merge/onboarding/claim path) takes a fresh live lease on branch `feature/x` — legitimately, since the worktree is now gone — by appending to the same log under the same lock; then this deferred code executes `git branch -d feature/x` (it is not checked out anywhere, so `-d` succeeds) and deletes the very branch the new lease was just placed on. The guard contract that "a claim appended between a survey and this call is seen" is therefore violated for the branch: the claim *is* appended after the survey and is *not* seen, because the branch deletion happens outside the lock that would have serialised it. `W.branch_exists` here also only checks existence, not protection, so even a branch that would have been refused by `_protected.why(...)` (e.g. an adopted tree's branch re-created in the window) gets removed; the resulting `Disposal("removed")` is reported as a clean success with no lease state consulted.

chunk_findings.detail:
The justification string passed to `dispose_tree` asserts two facts: "no uncommitted file" and "HEAD is the head the forge merged". The first is truly verified just above (the unconditional `_uncommitted`/`kept ... uncommitted files` check), but the second is only verified when `info.head_sha` is truthy:

    if info.head_sha and W.head_sha(path) != info.head_sha:
        return f"kept {path}: its HEAD is not the head that merged"

When the forge merge info has no `head_sha` (the guard exists precisely because this can be falsy/None), the HEAD comparison is short-circuited and never performed, yet the code still hands `forced_by="no uncommitted file, HEAD is the head the forge merged"` to a forced removal of the worktree. Whatever `dispose_tree` does with `forced_by` (it is the recorded reason for a destructive, force-removal action), the audit/log record will claim a HEAD verification that did not happen; e.g. an item whose `info.head_sha` is empty and whose local HEAD has since moved to a different commit is removed while the log states its "HEAD is the head the forge merged". The check should either be unconditional before this call, or the `forced_by` text should not claim a fact that was not established.

chunk_findings.detail:
This test is presented as the safeguard for the change's central guarantee ("a new caller of `worktree.remove` would be an unguarded, unlogged fifth path"), but it asserts on raw source text via two hard-coded spellings, so it is both unsound (false negatives) and brittle (false positives).

False negative: the guard only matches `W.remove(` and `worktree.remove(`. A new fifth path written in the most common style — `from ddflow.infra.worktree import remove` at the top of `ddflow/services/onboarding.py` followed by a bare `remove(path)` call — contains neither token, so `re.search` returns None, that file is not added to `callers`, and `assert callers == ["services/cleanup.py"]` still passes. The exact regression the test exists to catch ships green.

False positive: because it greps the whole file text (including comments, docstrings and string literals), any comment such as `# this used to call worktree.remove()` added to `services/merge.py`, or a docstring in `services/cleanup.py` describing the old path, makes `callers` include a file that never calls remove, failing the assertion and blocking a correct implementation. The check therefore neither proves the stated invariant when it passes nor reliably passes when the invariant holds.

chunk_findings.detail: The change updates `ddflow/config_sections/upgrade.py` to document that the refusal is install-dependent: an installed ddflow is told `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X`, while a source checkout is told to merge main (the intent quotes `Merge main into this checkout ... (ddflow >= X is needed)`). But the two places that actually recognise the guard still match only the installed phrasing (`upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X`). Concrete failure: a user running a source checkout against a project whose log was written by a newer ddflow triggers the skew guard; the write exits 3 with a message containing `Merge main into this checkout ... (ddflow >= X is needed)` and not the pinned substring. `templates/drivers/implement-phase.md` / `prompts/mcp_instructions.md` therefore fail to classify it as the skew refusal, so the driving agent does not take the documented recovery path (ask the user, offer `--allow-older-version/--reason`, or merge main) and will instead retry or misreport the failure — exactly the situation the doc change now advertises. The change has the install-neutral opener (`REFUSED: this project's log has been worked on by ddflow`) available to key on, and it chooses not to use it, leaving the code path that consumes the message out of sync with the message the doc now describes.
chunk_findings.title: templates/drivers/implement-phase.md, prompts/mcp_instructions.md (skew-guard recognition)

chunk_findings.detail: The diff updates the `upgrade.skew` doc to admit that the refusal message is now install-kind dependent: an installed ddflow still refuses with `Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X`, but a source checkout is told to "merge main ... (ddflow >= X is needed)". The agent-facing guard recognisers in `templates/drivers/implement-phase.md` and `prompts/mcp_instructions.md` are left pinning the literal `upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X` as the marker that identifies this guard. Concrete failure: a contributor runs ddflow from a source checkout whose log was last written by a newer `ddflow.seen` stamp, performs a write, and the guard refuses with a message that does not contain the pinned substring. The agent therefore does not recognise the refusal as the version-skew guard, skips the "ask the user; only if the user insists rerun with `--allow-older-version --reason ...`" branch, and treats it as a generic error — for exactly the environment (source checkout) that this change is about. Because the two skip paths now emit different openers, the recognisers must key off the install-neutral opener (`REFUSED: this project's log has been worked on by ddflow`) in the same change that makes the message heterogeneous; documenting the divergence without updating them leaves the guard unrecognisable for source checkouts.

chunk_findings.detail: The only runtime assertion this test makes is `skew_message(...).startswith(OPENER)`, where `OPENER` is the install-neutral prefix `"REFUSED: this project's log has been worked on by ddflow"`. That prefix is shared by *both* install kinds, so the statement passes whether or not the source-checkout branch is correct. The whole point of change (1) is that the *remedy* differs by install kind (installed → "Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X"; source checkout → "Merge main into this checkout …"), yet no test in this file ever asserts the remedy for either kind. Concretely: if the source-tree branch of `skew_message`/`upgrade_advice` were reverted to emit "…Upgrade ddflow-mcp to >= X…", iteration `kind == "source-tree"` would still satisfy `startswith(OPENER)` and the test would pass. The companion assertions in this file (`test_the_driver_and_the_instructions_recognise_the_guard_by_that_opener`, `test_the_skew_knob_doc_says_what_a_source_checkout_is_told`) read `KNOB_DOCS` and the markdown files, not the message, so they also pass with the reverted code. The install-kind loop therefore provides false confidence: it exercises the fabricated value `"source-tree"` but never demonstrates that a source checkout is actually told to merge main, which is the behavior the change is supposed to introduce.

chunk_findings.detail: The reader scan walks the AST for bare `ast.Name(id="FAMILY_HINTS")` / `ast.Attribute(attr="FAMILY_HINTS")` nodes, but an aliased import produces an `ast.alias` node, not a `Name`/`Attribute`. Concretely, if `ddflow/services/gates/reviewers.py` contained `from ..config import FAMILY_HINTS as _HINTS` and then used `_HINTS.get(...)`, the alias would never be visited as a `Name`/`Attribute`, `readers` would still be `[]`, and the test would pass while a second module read the shipped table — which is precisely the thing the docstring claims cannot happen ("no module reads the shipped hints table itself"). The same hole exists for `getattr(config, "FAMILY_HINTS")` (the name only appears as an `ast.Constant`). The check does not enforce its stated invariant.

chunk_findings.detail: `defs` and `readers` are built from `str(Path.relative_to(...))` and compared against POSIX-looking literals (`["services/gates/reviewers.py"]`, `[]`). On a POSIX-only CI this is latent, but there is nothing in the test pinning the separator.

data.claim: required gates were read from cfg.gates.required at 5 sites while GateDef.required was written only by load_gates (OR-only); a default-required gate dropped from the knob stayed True in its definition
data.falsifier: load_gates sets required False for a gate dropped from the knob

data.question: do the reviewer-gate and required-gate readers still disagree

chunk_findings.detail: `required_bad = [g for g in G.required_gates(cfg) if ...]` now iterates a `frozenset` instead of the config list, so the element order of `required_bad` is no longer the config order but the set's hash order, which for `str` elements is randomized per process (PYTHONHASHSEED is on by default). Concretely, with `[gates].required = ["b_verify", "a_verify"]` and both outcomes unsettled, one process can produce `["b_verify", "a_verify"]` and the next `["a_verify", "b_verify"]` for identical config and state, whereas before the change the order always followed the knob. Any consumer of this list that is order-sensitive — the emitted verdict/message text, a golden test, a recorded review artifact, or a cache/idempotency key derived from the result — will flap between identical runs. The fix is to preserve order at this site, e.g. `for g in cfg.gates.required if g in required_gates(cfg)` or by sorting `required_gates`' result before building `required_bad`.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/verify.py:274

chunk_findings.detail: `required_gates` has two modes that the change itself proves disagree: `test_a_definition_flagged_required_is_required` asserts `"extra" in G.required_gates(cfg, flagged)` while also asserting `"extra" not in G.required_gates(cfg)` for the same `cfg` (only the `gates` argument differs). The two call sites changed in this diff both take the one-argument form, i.e. they see only `[gates].required` and ignore `GateDef.required`. So for any gate whose definition says `required=True` but which is not listed in `[gates].required`, `required_gates(cfg, load_gates(repo, cfg))` reports it required while `required_gates(cfg)` reports it optional: `workflow.py:416` writes `required=False` into the GateDef it emits for that gate, and `markdown.py:680` builds `required = required_gates(cfg)` and then computes `todo = [g for g in pipeline_for(it, cfg) if not it.gate_satisfied(g, g in required)]`, so the unsatisfied gate is treated as satisfied and dropped from "gates remaining" (possibly printing "none — ready to complete"). The stated intent — one reader so that "every `GateDef.required` follows" the reader — is not achieved: asking `required_gates(cfg)` versus `required_gates(cfg, gates)` gives different answers for exactly the input the new test constructs. Either the one-arg call sites must pass the loaded definitions, or the definition-derived branch of the reader is unreachable via `load_gates` (in which case `test_a_definition_flagged_required_is_required` pins behaviour the production loader can never produce and gives false confidence).

chunk_findings.detail:
The new loop `for gid, gdef in gates.items(): gdef.required = gid in cfg.gates.required` unconditionally overwrites every definition's `required` field, including a value that came from the config overlay. Before this change the loop was `for gid in cfg.gates.required: if gid in gates: gates[gid].required = True` — it only ever raised the flag, so an explicit `required = true` on a gate definition survived `load_gates`. With an input such as

```toml
[gates]
required = []

[gate.extra]
required = true
```

`load_gates(cfg)["extra"].required` is now `False` (previously `True`), and consequently `G.required_gates(cfg, load_gates(cfg))` cannot ever include `extra`: the "plus any definition in `gates` flagged required" branch of `required_gates` (defs.py:405) is unreachable for any definition that came through the loader. This matters because the refutation offered for the earlier finding ("`load_gates` derives `GateDef.required` from the knob, so flagged is a subset") is circular: `required_gates(cfg, load_gates(...)) == required_gates(cfg)` holds only because `load_gates` destroys the flag, not because the two sources agree. The probe `test_a_definition_flagged_required_is_required` that is said to demonstrate the honouring passes a synthetic `flagged` mapping, so it never exercises the overlay path and would still pass if the honouring code did nothing. Net effect: the stated intent that `required_gates` honours `GateDef.required` is not delivered for any real config, and a previously effective per-gate `required = true` is silently dropped.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/gates/defs.py:396 (`load_gates`)

chunk_findings.detail: The old body was `head = _last_head(log, it.id, gate) if it else ""`, i.e. it explicitly tolerated a falsy `it` and returned the empty diff/refusal tuple. The refactor removes that guard and calls `_last_head(it, gate)` unconditionally, while `_last_head` now takes the `Item` (per the intent: “_full_rounds/_delta_rounds/_last_head/_last_review now take the Item”) and therefore dereferences the item (e.g. `it.gate_history`) to find the recorded head. There is a reachable path with `it is None`: the caller resolves the item with `st.items.get(item)` (the same pattern used at the `_any_out_of_rounds(cfg, st.items.get(item), …)` call, which explicitly handles `None` via `if it is None: return False`), so an item id that is absent from `st.items` (or a repo-scoped/`--delta` invocation with no item) passes `None` here. With `it=None` the old code returned the “no recorded review” empty-diff result; the new code raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'gate_history'` inside `_last_head`. The fix is to keep the guard (`_last_head(it, gate) if it else ""`) or make `_last_head` return `""` for `it is None`.

chunk_findings.detail:
The removed per-event code only short-circuited on `outcome == "started"`:

```python
if outcome == "started":
    return
r.gate_outcomes.setdefault(d.get("gate", "?"), []).append(outcome)
r.add_gate_run(...)
```

so any other value carried in the event's `outcome` field — including `out_of_order` — was folded into `r.gate_outcomes` and into the record's gate runs. The replacement derives these from `Item.gate_history`, and `GateRun`'s own docstring states that «The log's `started` and `out_of_order` events are not outcomes and are not here», i.e. `gate_history` will not contain an entry for an `out_of_order` gate event.

Failure scenario: a log containing a gate event whose `outcome` is `out_of_order` (the same stream that yields `outcome == "started"`, which is why the old handler tested for it). Old behaviour: `r.gate_outcomes["<gate>"]` gets an `"out_of_order"` entry and `r` gets a corresponding gate run. New behaviour: the loop at progress.py:296 iterates only `it.gate_history`, so that entry/run silently disappears for both `r.gate_outcomes` and `add_gate_run`. That contradicts the stated "Behaviour must be identical", and the log-scan oracle (which sees every non-`started` outcome) would disagree with the folded result on such a log. Either the fold in `handlers/gates.py` must also record `out_of_order` runs, or the derived loop cannot reproduce the old scan.

chunk_findings.detail: The old implementation had an explicit filter that discarded `out_of_order` outcomes (`if outcome == "out_of_order": continue`) and skipped `gate.started` events. The new loop copies every `run.outcome` out of `Item.gate_history` into `GateRate.outcomes` with no equivalent guard. Given a state whose history contains an `out_of_order` run for a gate (e.g. a `gate.out_of_order` event recorded during a pipeline-order complaint), the new `gate_rates` counts that run as a real outcome, inflating `GateRate.runs` and skewing the pass/fail rate, whereas the old function deliberately ignored it as “not a verdict about the work.” The docstring asserts that fold excludes these runs, but `gate_rates` does not enforce that invariant and also accepts an arbitrary `State`, so any state carrying such a run produces the wrong rate.

chunk_findings.detail: `_delta_scope` previously read the last head as `head = _last_head(log, it.id, gate) if it else ""`; the diff replaces it with the unguarded `head = _last_head(it, gate)`. The new `_last_head` takes the `Item` and (per the intent: `_full_rounds/_delta_rounds/_last_head/_last_review now take the Item`) must dereference it, e.g. `it.gate_history`, so `it is None` now raises `AttributeError` where the old code returned `""` and fell through to the function's own graceful `if not head: return ("", how, why_not)` branch that the body explicitly documents. Concretely, calling `_delta_scope(repo, None, gate, branch)` (i.e. `--delta` reached with an item id that is not resolved into an `Item` in `st.items`) used to yield the "no recorded review head" diff tuple and now crashes. The sibling hunk at `review.py:1002` is the same mismatch: it keeps the old condition `... if ref and item else ""` (keyed on the *string* `item`) but now passes the *object* `it` to `_last_head`, so an item id that is present while the corresponding `Item` is missing still takes the unguarded path. Either the guard must be reinstated (`... if it else ""`, keyed on `it`) or `_last_head` must explicitly tolerate `it is None`; as written, the two call sites disagree with the only None check newly added nearby (`_any_out_of_rounds` does `if it is None: return False`), which shows the authors know `it` can be absent.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_delta_scope

chunk_findings.detail: The fold `r.gate_outcomes.setdefault(run.gate or "?", []).append(run.outcome)` / `r.add_gate_run(...)` replaces the removed per-event lines that ran for *every* event outcome except `started`. The replaced code did **not** skip `out_of_order`; only `started` was filtered (`if outcome == "started": return`). But the new `GateRun` docstring defines `gate_history` as holding outcomes only, explicitly stating "the log's `started` and `out_of_order` events ... are not here". Concrete input: a log containing a gate event `{"gate": "review", "outcome": "out_of_order", ...}` (and no preceding `started` for that subject). Old code produced `gate_outcomes["review"] == ["out_of_order"]` and a corresponding `add_gate_run` entry; the new code produces no entry at all, because that outcome never enters `gate_history`. Since `services/rates.gate_rates` and the review round counters now read exactly this structure (and `tests/test_gate_history.py` encodes the old scan as its oracle), any rate/count that included `out_of_order` now silently drops it, so behaviour is not identical.

chunk_findings.detail: The old implementation of `_last_review` read evidence as `ev = e.data.get("evidence") or {}` before testing `ev.get("reviewed_head")`; the new implementation dropped that guard and does `if r.evidence.get("reviewed_head")` directly on the `GateRun`. A `gate.claim` (re-claim) or `gate.skip` event carries no evidence, which is precisely the case the old `or {}` was defending against and precisely the case the new docstring still claims to support ("a re-claim or `gate skip` replaces the gate's current record"). If the fold stores such a run with `evidence` unset/`None` (as the log event itself did), then for a history like `[review run with reviewed_head, claim run without evidence]` the `reversed(...)` loop hits the claim run first and `r.evidence.get("reviewed_head")` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get'` instead of falling through to the reviewed run / returning `{}`. The old log scan survived exactly this sequence (and the `_last_head` docstring says a delta must stay possible after a re-claim/skip), so this is a behavioral regression introduced by the port, not a pre-existing condition. Either restore `(r.evidence or {}).get(...)` or guarantee `GateRun.evidence` is always a dict.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review.py:_last_review

chunk_findings.detail:
The replaced loop was guarded by `gid in gates`:

```python
for gid, spec in (data.get("gate") or {}).items():
    if gid in gates and isinstance(spec, dict) and "human" in spec:
        gates[gid].human = bool(spec["human"])
```

so an overlay entry naming a gate the loaded config does not define never entered `gates`. The helper this now calls is the same one used a few lines up (line ~178), where it *must* create entries — the comment there explains that a gate defined "in the very same call" has to be materialised, and the old code it replaces did `g = gates.get(gid) or GateDef(id=gid)`. Passing `only=("human",)` only whitelists the *field* (`human`), it does not reinstate the "gate must already exist" guard, so `apply_gate_table` will also insert a fresh `GateDef` for an overlay-only gate id. Concrete case: predecessor config has a pipeline list referencing a gate with no `[gate.X]` table (`gates.deploy_pipeline = ["approve"]`, no `[gate.approve]`), and the candidate layer adds `[gate.approve] human = true`. Old code: `approve` not in `gates`, so it is excluded and the derived set is `{}`. New code: `approve` is created with `human = true`, `pipelined(cfg)` already yields it, and `gates["approve"].is_human_gate` is true, so the set of human-gated pipelines now includes `approve` — a sign-off gate appears that the previous implementation did not report. The `only` tuple narrows the fields written, not the set of gate ids that get created.

chunk_findings.detail: The rewrite of the human-gate overlay silently drops the guards the removed loop carried. The old code was `if gid in gates and isinstance(spec, dict) and "human" in spec: gates[gid].human = bool(spec["human"])` — it only *modified existing* gates. The replacement, `WF.apply_gate_table(gates, data.get("gate") or {}, only=("human",))`, reuses the helper that the other call site (lines 168–178) depends on for the opposite behavior: that call site's own comment says it must materialize gates "defined in the very same call" so that "defining `lint` and piping it in one command" no longer "refused itself for naming an undefined gate." So the shared helper necessarily does `g = gates.get(gid) or GateDef(id=gid)` and then `gates[gid] = g`, and no value of `only` (which filters *fields*, not gate ids) can re-impose the `gid in gates` restriction. chunk_findings.detail:
The guard only admits a file into `homes` when its text literally contains `"CLAUDECODE"` or `"def agent_marker"`. But the rule the test claims to pin is more than the harness var: it is the precedence `requested` → `DDFLOW_AGENT` → harness marker → `""`. A second copy that re-uses identity's data but re-implements the precedence — `from .identity import HARNESS_MARKERS` (so the literal `CLAUDECODE` never appears) plus a `DDFLOW_AGENT` check, and named anything other than `agent_marker` — contains neither token, so `homes` remains `{"services/identity.py"}` and the assertion passes while a private duplicate of the rule exists. Concretely, adding to `ddflow/services/rules.py`:

```python
def pick_marker(req):
    if req: return f"--agent {req}"
    if os.environ.get("DDFLOW_AGENT"): return "DDFLOW_AGENT=" + os.environ["DDFLOW_AGENT"]
    for v in ID.HARNESS_MARKERS:
        if v in os.environ: return f"{v} is set"
    return ""
```

keeps the test green even though this is exactly the "second env-var check" drift the docstring says the test is meant to catch. The test's name/promise (`defines_or_reads_the_agent_marker`) is therefore stronger than what it actually enforces: it pins only one possible spelling of a duplicate (hardcoded `CLAUDECODE`, or a function literally named `agent_marker`), so a duplicate keyed on `DDFLOW_AGENT` (or on a harness var pulled from `HARNESS_MARKERS`) is invisible.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new `resolve()` implements the `DDFLOW_AGENT` layer as a *provenance* test — `getattr(cfg, "sources", {}).get("agent.id", "default") == "default"` — while its own docstring states the rule as a *value* test: "`DDFLOW_AGENT` (only while `[agent].id` is just its default)". These disagree whenever a config file sets the default value explicitly, and the failure is observable.

Concrete input: `DDFLOW_AGENT=bob` in the environment, config file containing `[agent].id = ""`. Then `cfg.sources["agent.id"]` is the config filename (not `"default"`), so the env branch is skipped; `getattr(getattr(cfg, "agent", None), "id", "")` is `""` (falsy), so the config branch is skipped too; the function returns `AgentId(default_agent_id(root), "derived")`. Per the documented ordering, the config value *is* the default, so layer 2 (`DDFLOW_AGENT`) should have applied and the result should be `AgentId("bob", "env")`. An env var the harness exported is silently discarded and the tree-derived name is used for writes instead.

The same source-vs-value mismatch fails in the other direction: when `cfg` carries no source tracking (`sources` absent or missing the `"agent.id"` key — which the `getattr(..., {})` fallback explicitly anticipates), the default `"default"` is assumed, so `return AgentId(env, "env")` fires even though `cfg.agent.id` may be an explicitly configured value; e.g. cfg with `agent.id = "alice"` and empty `sources` plus `DDFLOW_AGENT=bob` yields `bob`/`"env"` instead of `alice`/`"config"`. The guard needs to test the effective value (or a real `is_default` helper), not infer it from a source map that may be absent or keyed differently.
